title: Outsourced Large-Load Intake Desk for Co-op Pools
one_liner: A stage-gated, applicant-paid intake administrator and cross-utility duplicate registry for G&T co-op pools outside ERCOT, so 5-person planning staffs only ever see evidence-backed projects.
customer: Wedge: one mid-size G&T (or state co-op association planning group) outside ERCOT, in SPP, MISO or the Mountain West, that fields 8+ large-load inquiries a year and has 1-2 planners eating the load (Central Electric Power Cooperative's lead spends about 40% of his time on data centers). The G&T adopts the desk by board resolution, and the applicant pays through a filed fee schedule, following Great River Energy's bill-the-petitioner model. Second ring: the G&T's 20-40 distribution co-ops, then neighboring G&Ts.
problem: The judges' central worry was right. Collateral, study fees and site-control rules are making applicants self-prove, so a 12-point memo shop sells checks the applicant will soon hand over anyway. Equipment slots and financing letters are also confidential, and real developers often call the utility before they order equipment. Meanwhile the co-op still has no staff to run intake and no way to see that the same 300 MW is being shopped to five utilities. Regulators are absorbing LLC transparency at the state level (Texas audit, Pennsylvania's Aug 18 order for projects over 25 MW), which weakens any pure-LLC-lookup product.
solution: Run intake as an operated service, not a memo. (1) Evidence ladder tied to money release. Gate 0 (intake fee paid): public-record checks only, which is what any real developer already has: LLC principals across states, recorded deed or option, air-permit pre-application and generator count vs. claimed MW, water and stormwater filings, and claimed energization date vs. published transformer and switchgear lead times. Gate 1 (study deposit released): named references (OEM, EPC, tenant, lender officer) verified by phone, with a signed attestation and a misrepresentation clause that forfeits the deposit. Gate 2 (ESA signature): redacted OEM order acknowledgment and financing confirmation. Early gates test only what an early-stage real project has; unobservable items are pushed to the gate where money is at risk. (2) Consent clause: the application form has the applicant consent to share LLC, principals, parcel APN, POI substation, MW ask and status with a pooled registry, which solves the confidentiality problem. The registry matches on parcel, substation POI and principal, not company name, because shells rename themselves but land parcels and substations do not. It returns hits like 'this parcel and principal appear in 3 other territories.' (3) Outputs are structured records that drop into GridUnity or PowerClerk as the pre-queue front door.
why_now: Tariffs and collateral rules are landing (Texas SB 6 final rule due by 12/31/2026, AEP Ohio-style deposits), and Exelon's pipeline fell about 40% and AEP Ohio's more than half once fees and collateral arrived. Every co-op now has to decide what its intake rules are, and most have no staff to run them. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so boards are burned. Cleanview-class permit data has made the public-record layer cheap to assemble and license. Nobody yet runs a duplicate registry outside ERCOT, where SB 6 mandates duplicate disclosure only inside the state.
revenue_model: $20-30K one-time G&T setup (intake policy, fee schedule, ESA rider, board presentation). Applicant-paid intake fees scaled by MW, $10K under 100 MW up to $40K over 500 MW, plus a $15-30K Gate 1 verification fee. The utility keeps a 15% admin share and the desk keeps 85%. A $36K/yr G&T floor retainer covers slow quarters. Registry seats at $12K/yr for utilities outside the pool later. Bottom-up: 3 G&Ts x about 25 paid intakes x about $20K is $1.5M in year 1 at about 80% gross margin, with the registry as the compounding asset.
non_obvious_insight: The fee and the gates are themselves the phantom filter. Shell LLCs will not pay $15K to be verified, and real developers spending $2B+ will not blink. So the desk's real product is converting scarce planner hours into a queue that carries only evidence-backed projects, and detection is a side effect. The staged ladder fixes the 'real developers come before they order equipment' flaw by demanding equipment proof only at the gate where the utility's money is at risk. And the registry keys on parcels and POI substations, physical objects a phantom cannot rename, which is why it holds up even as LLC-disclosure rules improve.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: get the last 10-15 inquiries from two co-op contacts via a state association or G&T planning group. Back-test them to show how the ones that died would have scored at Gate 0 and Gate 1. Stand up scrapers for air-permit databases in 4-6 states and deed and Secretary of State records in 2-3 territories, and license Cleanview-style permit data instead of rebuilding it. Days 10-20: write the 2-page intake policy, fee schedule and misrepresentation-clause template. Present the back-test and template to the G&T planning head and ask for a 90-day pilot that starts fees on the next new inquiry, free for existing ones. Days 20-30: interview 5 developers with real projects to test that they would pay $10-15K at intake. Close 1 G&T pilot and process the first paid intake. Kill test: if no G&T will let applicants be billed, or 0 of 5 real developers accept the fee, the applicant-pays thesis is dead.
lineage: mutation of I0079 ('Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GridUnity, Clean Power Research (PowerClerk), Enverus, LandGate. White space: I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check. | How this version avoids them: GridUnity and PowerClerk are workflow tools built on applicant-supplied data. The desk verifies and feeds them as a front door, so it is a complement to sell alongside, not a rival. Enverus, LandGate, GridCARE and ZEG sit on the developer side or in forecasting, and this desk works for the utility and is adverse to the applicant. Cleanview is a public tracker and cannot hold confidential cross-utility inquiry data, so it becomes a licensed input rather than a competitor. NRECA offers free checklists but cannot run a fee-collecting, data-holding, liability-bearing intake operation, so its state associations are the resale channel. Hourly consultancies (Burns & McDonnell and similar) could copy the checks but not the pooled registry economics. Memos were the entry product; the pooled registry across co-ops is the business, and it gets better with every co-op added.

title: IEP Chief of Staff for Special-Ed Parents
one_liner: Rich parents win school disputes with a paid educational advocate and paper trail; for $20/mo, give parents of the roughly 7.5M US students with IEPs a chief of staff who watches the legal clocks and logs every missed service minute.
customer: Parents of children with IEPs (autism, ADHD, dyslexia, speech and language delay), sold through state and local special-ed parent groups, parent training centers, pediatric practices, disability law clinics and credit unions.
problem: Districts arrive with a team; wealthy families bring an advocate ($150-400/hr) and an attorney. Federal enforcement was hollowed out (mass OSEP layoffs in October 2025, and reported moves of oversight to HHS and civil-rights enforcement to DOJ in June 2026), so parents are effectively on their own. Most violations are procedural (late evaluations, missing prior written notice, services not delivered) and go unnoticed because nobody keeps the clocks.
solution: Parent uploads the IEP and evaluations. The system builds the legal calendar (evaluation timelines from consent, meeting-notice windows, annual and triennial reviews, progress-report cadence), drafts records requests, creates a one-page pre-meeting brief (top asks plus data), and sends a same-day 'memorializing' follow-up email with prior-written-notice requests after meetings. It logs service minutes delivered vs promised, quantifying missed minutes for a compensatory-services claim, and scans the IEP for defects (no baselines, unmeasurable goals). Advocates are on-demand at $75 per 30 minutes, with a path to state complaint and due process.
why_now: The federal special-ed enforcement vacuum is documented and new as of late 2025 and mid-2026. IEP counts are rising, and LLMs can parse messy IEP PDFs and draft procedurally precise letters. Parent communities are organized on Facebook and Reddit and actively looking for help.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family; $75 advocate sessions with a revenue split to a vetted advocate co-op; $3-6 per member per month from parent centers, pediatric groups and credit unions; district-facing analytics sold only with parent consent, later.
non_obvious_insight: What the rich buy is not better argument but continuous procedural pressure: dated, written, specific requests. The subscription funds clock-watching and documentation, not advice. Parents who log service minutes turn 'I feel they're not delivering' into a quantified claim, and the paper trail is the evidence in any later dispute, so value compounds over time.
first_30_days: Publish a free IEP clock calculator and letter templates. Partner with admins of 10 state-level special-ed Facebook groups and concierge 30 families manually, measuring violations found. Convert those families to $20/mo and recruit 5 advocates for the on-demand tier.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: IEP Advocate.ai, ChatGPT and general LLMs (endorsed by CADRE's parent guide), Parent Training and Information Centers (PTIs/CPRCs), Wrightslaw. White space: Confidence is moderate-low. The WebSearch budget hit 200/200 before I could run the planned 6-12 searches, so I found competitors mostly by fetching guessed and known URLs. More direct competitors probably exist that I did not see, and this should be re-run once the search limit is raised.

The core pitch is NOT white space. Deadline extraction, procedural letter generation, meeting prep briefs and state-complaint drafting are already live at IEP Advocate.ai for $30/mo. Free ChatGPT covers much of the rest. A $20/mo 'AI IEP chief of staff' would be a cheaper copy.

Specific gaps I could not find served in the pages I reached:
1. A service-delivery ledger. This means logging minutes promised vs delivered per IEP service line and turning the shortfall into a compensatory-services claim packet. IEP Advocate.ai's fetched pages do not describe service-minute logging or comp-ed calculation.
2. Human-in-the-loop verification. CADRE and K-12 Dive document AI-drafted complaints with fabricated case law and wrong IDEA readings. A product that combines grounded output with vetted advocate or attorney review, at $75 per 30 minutes, is unserved. IEP Advocate.ai has no human tier.
3. B2B2C distribution through parent centers, disability law clinics, pediatric practices and credit unions at $3-6 per member per month. IEP Advocate.ai lists only individual pricing. The channel is unproven.
4. Evidence-grade record keeping. Time-stamped, tamper-evident logs that a hearing officer will accept, rather than chat history.

title: Ruling-Backed Tariff Engineering for Product Brands
one_liner: A productized design-and-ruling service that helps mid-market brands legitimately re-spec products across tariff-line boundaries and locks the result in with a CBP binding ruling.
customer: Mid-market consumer and industrial product brands with $10-100M in revenue and at least $1-2M in annual duty spend: footwear, bags, apparel accessories, home goods, hardware, e-bike and powersports parts, and other products with metal components.
problem: Adjacent tariff lines can differ by tens of percentage points, and the 2025-26 regime made the gaps bigger. Section 232 metals lists keep expanding and being recalibrated, and copper smelt-and-cast reporting started July 30, 2026. Yet brokers are asked for a classification only after the tooling is cut and the design is frozen. Product teams never learn that a small change in materials, construction, packaging or set composition can legally change the line. Importers also avoid asking CBP for rulings, assuming it is slow or risky.
solution: Sell two steps. First, a fixed-fee HTS boundary audit: map the top SKUs to the classification tests, spec thresholds and comparable public CBP rulings that determine the line, and list the small design or packaging changes that would legitimately move each one. Second, an engineering sprint with the supplier that documents the changed product and files a CBP binding ruling request under 19 CFR Part 177. The deliverable is a ruling letter, which is a lasting shield for reasonable-care defense. Add a ruling-watch subscription that alerts brands when CBP issues a ruling on competitor or adjacent products.
why_now: The IEEPA reversal shifted the burden to product-specific tariffs (Section 232 and 301) where design details matter. The July 2026 copper reporting and the rewritten 232 valuation rules make product composition a compliance and cost variable. Brands are in a rare window when rate spreads are large enough that redesign pays for itself in one production run.
revenue_model: $4,500 boundary audit for five SKUs; $18-35k per engineering sprint including ruling preparation and filing; optional success fee of about 10% of first-year duty savings, capped. Ruling-watch subscription of $500-$2,000 a month.
non_obvious_insight: Classification turns on physical facts of the article as imported, and those facts are set by designers, not brokers. The most valuable document in a tariff war is a dull letter from CBP's ruling office, and requests cost nothing to file. Tariff engineering is legal when the product really changes, and it requires evidence, which is where a broker's habit of documenting everything matters. Trade lawyers do this ad hoc for large clients, but nobody packages it for mid-market brands at design stage.
first_30_days: Pick two verticals with high design freedom and large rate spreads. Use public CBP rulings to build a boundary map for a prospect's own top SKU as a free sample. Cold-email 40 product, sourcing and COO leads at $10-100M brands with their own sample map. Sell three $4,500 boundary audits and use them to select the first ruling filings. Sign a trade lawyer as reviewing counsel on the ruling requests.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Tarifflo, Flexport (Customs Suite, AI Customs Classification, trade advisory, tariff refund claims), Zonos (Classify), Trademo (Global Trade Management). White space: Verified by fetches, with caveats below. No fetched page showed anyone selling a packaged, fixed-fee, design-stage (pre-tooling) HTS boundary audit for mid-market product brands ($10-100M revenue). None showed a bundled CBP binding-ruling filing with counsel review, or a ruling-watch product built on comparable-ruling analysis.

Software players (Zonos, Trademo, Descartes, Flexport) classify existing products. Tarifflo recovers past overpayments. Big-4 and law firms sell hourly advisory to large clients. A mid-market design-team buyer at the pre-tooling stage looks unserved.

Caveats that cap confidence:
1. The 200-call web search budget ran out before any search ran. Nothing was searched for boutique tariff-engineering consultancies, startups, YC or Crunchbase entries, Product Hunt, or open-source tools.
2. Several vendor fetches failed or returned thin pages: Altana, Avalara, Sandler Travis, Crowell, KPMG, Thomson Reuters, Expeditors and CROSS features.
3. So 'nobody does this exactly' is unproven. A specialist boutique or a well-funded new entrant may exist.

Structural risks that shrink the white space:
- Per 19 CFR 177.2, CBP rulings are limited to prospective transactions and require a full factual statement, samples and photos.
- Per 19 CFR 177.9, a ruling binds CBP only for the addressee and only for identical articles. Third parties cannot rely on it, and CBP can modify or revoke it without notice to anyone else.
- A classification ruling does not protect against Section 232 list changes. The lists are recalibrated and CBP treats sets by their primary classifying article. Redesigning across a line can be undone if the new line is later added to the list.

title: Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data
one_liner: An audit that tells research buyers what share of their online-panel responses came from bots, agents or fraud farms, and recalibrates the study against a verified-human control sample.
customer: Insights heads at CPG, pharma and financial-services firms, UX-research teams, academic labs and pollsters who buy panel sample from third-party vendors at $5-500 per complete.
problem: One prompt to a commercial AI agent now passes screeners and attention checks. A controlled evaluation found synthetic respondents passing 99.8% of 6,000 attention-check trials. As little as 3-7% contaminated responses can invalidate conclusions. Panel vendors both sell the sample and score its quality, so buyers cannot trust the referee.
solution: A per-study data-quality audit. Response files (timings, paradata, device data, open-ends) go through a detection ensemble plus honeypot items. A subset of the same questionnaire goes to a small address-recruited, device-attested human panel as a ground-truth control. Deliver an audit stamp, contamination-adjusted estimates, and a vendor scorecard across suppliers.
why_now: Survey-fraud research in 2025-26 shows agents beating attention checks. An MIT-run $50K challenge is testing detection, and NORC published a fraud literature review. Election-season polling and pharma sample budgets raise the stakes, and buyers are asking who audits the panels.
revenue_model: $3-15k per study audit, $50-150k per year programmes for insights teams that spend $2-10M on sample, and vendor-scorecard subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Most anti-fraud tooling is sold by panel sellers, whose incentive is to under-report fraud. The scarce asset is not detection code but an independent, verified-human comparison group, because you cannot prove what is fake without a known-real reference.
first_30_days: Recruit about 2,000 verified humans by address-based mail or a university survey-centre partnership. Buy sample from six panel vendors yourself and publish a 'state of sample quality' benchmark. Offer free audits to five insights leaders who have posted about bad data.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Data Quality Co-op (DQC), Verasight, Verisoul, CloudResearch (Sentry, Engage, Bot Olympics). White space: Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight.

title: Remote Load Calcs That Avoid Panel Upgrades
one_liner: A photo-and-utility-bill service that proves an existing electrical panel can take a heat pump or EV charger, with load-management devices when it cannot.
customer: HVAC and heat-pump contractors, EV-charger installers and solar-plus-storage installers without in-house electricians. Later: state and utility electrification programs.
problem: Data centers are absorbing electricians (nearly a third of the shortage; Texas builders report electrical delays of up to 2 months). Residential electrician time becomes the scarcest input, so panel upgrades stall every electrification job. HVAC contractors selling heat pumps are blocked by work they do not do and cannot schedule. The HVAC rebound expected in 2027 will make it worse.
solution: Installer uploads a photo of the panel label plus 12 months of utility data. The service returns a permit-ready load calculation under the existing-load method, stamped by a remote licensed engineer or electrician. It recommends the cheapest path: no upgrade, a load-management or circuit-pausing device allowed by recent NEC editions, or a smart panel, with the material list for the installer's quote.
why_now: Electrician scarcity from data-center overtime ($130-170K, vendor stat), 2027 HVAC rebound with A2L certification adding friction, and a 110K technician shortage. Load-management devices and energy-management provisions are now commercially available and code-recognized in many places.
revenue_model: $79-149 per calculation billed to installers. Annual contracts with programs. Referral margin from load-management device makers.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for electrification is neither the heat pump nor the HVAC tech, it is the panel and the electrician-days it consumes. Avoiding electrician hours is worth more than adding them, and the existing truck-roll panel check can be done as a $99 desk job by one remote engineer serving many installers.
first_30_days: Sign 20 HVAC contractors in one state. Contract a licensed PE or master electrician for templates and stamps. Deliver 50 calculations by hand. Measure the percentage that avoided an upgrade.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TrueLoad (eTherm Solutions LLC), TradesQuote (rajesh99/tradesquote-website), PanelWright (open source), SPAN (PowerUp / smart panel). White space: The market is not empty: TrueLoad already sells software-only NEC 220.87 reports from utility interval data to heat pump and EV installers at $30/project, and the underlying calc is even open-source. The white space is what TrueLoad says it does not do, plus the liability-bearing layer nobody has bundled. (1) A stamped, licensed-professional deliverable. Small HVAC and EV contractors without in-house electricians must take on risk when they self-certify a software report, and WattMonk shows they pay for stamped desk work in solar. (2) Photo-of-panel intake, so installers do not hand-key service details. (3) A cheapest-path recommendation with a compliant load-management spec and bill of materials (NEC 625.42 EVEMS, 750 energy management, 705.13 power control systems), which TrueLoad explicitly lacks and hardware vendors only offer for their own products. (4) Doing the utility interval-data retrieval for the contractor, which is the real friction, since TrueLoad's own guides tell users to request it themselves. (5) HVAC and heat-pump contractors as the buyer, with a pre-check integrated into state or utility programs. Weak points: a $79-149 price against a $30 software anchor needs the stamp and outcome to justify a 3-5x premium; solar desks like WattMonk or Aurora can add this as a SKU; and I could not verify Qmerit or unknown small engineering shops.

title: Record-on-Request Desk for Superior Courts
one_liner: A managed compliance service that lets a superior court answer any indigent litigant's request for a verbatim record with one certified record per request, priced per record delivered and using the cheapest lawful method, whether steno or electronic recording.
customer: Court executive officers and presiding family/probate judges of small and mid-size California superior courts, especially those outside the AB 3013 pilot or above its 10-20% cap. Self-represented litigants and DV legal aid are the users, but the court is the payer.
problem: FVAP v. Superior Court (Aug 10, 2026) gives indigent litigants a mandatory right to an official verbatim record on request, through court-paid pro tem reporters or electronic recording. Courts have no reporters and hiring freezes, and they cannot staff for requests that could arrive any day. Their real gap is a defensible request-to-record workflow: intake, indigency check, method selection, delivery of a certified appeal-ready record, and reporting. The 3 million hearings without a record are already a Judicial Council-visible metric. Half-day pro tem minimums make each request cost $450-500 or more.
solution: A per-request desk, priced by outcome. The litigant or facilitator files a request when they set the hearing, so the desk usually gets 2-7 days of notice, which turns random demand into schedulable demand. The desk picks the method: (a) the court's own recording plus a certified transcript on demand (subcontracted to an eScribers-style vendor), or (b) a physically present steno reporter from a pooled roster that covers several requests in the same courthouse (the offspring-1 network) when a steno record is required or the department has no recording. The court pays only for records delivered and certified. A dashboard shows requests, turnaround and no-record rate by department, ready for Judicial Council reporting. The desk is offered at no retainer with a quarterly spend cap, sized to the court's own budget.
why_now: The Supreme Court decision is Aug 2026 and the court decision names the compliance routes, so every court now needs a plan, and no incumbent has packaged one. Reporter budgets and vacancy savings exist because courts cannot fill positions, and CA has already sent dedicated funding to court reporters (verify the current allocation and whether vacancy savings can be redirected). Verbit's Judicial Council master agreement for captioning from July 1, 2026 shows courts do buy court-tech through master agreements, which gives a path from single-court pilots to statewide.
revenue_model: The court pays a flat $150-250 per hearing record delivered (up to 30 minutes), certified transcripts at a per-page rate, and no retainer. Pricing sits below a $450-500 half-day pro tem and far below an idle full-time reporter. Steno requests use pooled reporters, and audio requests use subcontracted transcription, so gross margin is about 30-40%. Year 2: annual subscription for the dashboard and intake software, and a statewide master-agreement bid. Legal aid and foundations can fund 'request navigators' who file requests for litigants, which lifts volume.
non_obvious_insight: The court does not need reporters. It needs a defensible answer to a request, so the method is irrelevant, and the biggest threat (electronic recording) becomes a supply input to a desk that will choose it. Requests that arrive at intake instead of at the courtroom door are what make pooled steno economical, because notice converts unpredictable demand into a schedule. Outcome pricing ('pay only when a certified record is delivered') is the contingency that lets a risk-averse court say yes without a retainer.
first_30_days: Week 1: one-week legal check with a court-reporter licensing attorney, plus reading the ruling's list of lawful compliance routes. Weeks 1-3: ask FVAP and 2-3 DV legal-aid groups to introduce court executives of two counties with the highest no-record rates. Build the intake form and an eScribers-style subcontract, and sign 3 physical pro tem reporters in one county. Weeks 3-4: offer one family department a no-cost, at-cost 60-day compliance pilot (about 20-40 requests) with a weekly report. Aim for an under-threshold purchase order or sole-source urgent-compliance pilot within 90-120 days. The 30-day success test is a signed pilot letter from one court and a design-partner agreement with FVAP.
lineage: mutation of I0248 ('Fifteen-Minute Court Reporting for Family Law Hearings'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Steno (Steno Agency Inc.), DirectDep, StenoScout, Incumbent agencies (Veritext, Esquire, Combs Reporting, Coalition Court Reporters). White space: Nobody offers flat-fee coverage of 15-minute California family-law hearings. That is because the core mechanic, private reporters dialing in from anywhere, is currently barred. Gov. Code 69959 says 'Remote court reporting shall not be used by courts to make the record of any court proceedings' and defines it as a stenographer not present in the courtroom (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959/). The only exception, Gov. Code 69959.5, allows remote reporting only by 'full-time official reporters ... employed by the participating superior court', physically in a court facility, in 13 pilot counties, capped at 10-20% of reporters (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959-5/). San Diego's court page states 'the court is prohibited by law from allowing remote court reporting for any court proceeding' (https://sdcourt.ca.gov/sdcourt/generalinformation/resourcelists/courtreporterinformation). The idea's claim that AB 3013 'opened remote reporting' to a private platform is wrong. Unserved and still legal: (1) physical-presence short-hearing coverage, where one pro tem covers several departments in the same courthouse using calendar-based duration prediction, and no vendor markets a per-hearing SKU; (2) a scheduling and utilization layer sold to courts to fill pro tem and official reporter slots, aimed at hiring and retention (the ruling names 'pro tem reporters paid by the court' as a compliance route, and court reporter counsel is calling on courts to lift hiring freezes); (3) fast certified transcripts of court electronic recordings for attorneys who need appellate-grade records. The white space is real but is a legal-regime bet on remote reporting being opened to private reporters, plus a narrow physical-hopping wedge. It is not a software-only wedge. Court reporter unions opposed AB 3013 and are a political headwind. | How this version avoids them: Steno, DirectDep and StenoScout sell to attorneys, mostly depositions, and have no intake, indigency, certification or reporting workflow for courts. The incumbent agencies sell courts half-day pro tem bookings, which is the price the desk undercuts. eScribers and Verbit transcribe recordings but do not handle request intake, method choice or physical steno backup, so they are supply partners, not rivals. The AB 3013 pilot is court-employed, capped and in 13 counties; we serve every court above the cap or outside the pilot. The main threat is a court building intake in-house or a Judicial Council master agreement commoditizing the service, so the plan is to be on the master agreement's vendor list early and to own the request-intake data.

title: Referee Sampling for Black Mass and Battery Scrap
one_liner: Independent sampling and assay of black mass lots, using Pierre Gy's Theory of Sampling from mining, so scrap sellers and recyclers stop fighting over 5-15% payable swings.
customer: Battery-scrap sellers who are paid by assay: gigafactory scrap desks, EV and ESS dismantlers, and shredder pre-processors in Germany, Poland, the US Midwest, Ontario and Korea. Buyers are hydromet recyclers and trading houses that want defensible acceptance. Whoever needs the settlement pays $1.5-4k per lot or $15-40 per tonne, and often splits it.
problem: Black mass is a worst-case heterogeneous powder: coarse Cu and Al foil flakes, plastic, residual electrolyte, graphite, and a nugget effect for Ni, Co and Cu. Payables are computed on the assay of a few grams. Anyone from mining knows 90% or more of assay error is sampling error (fundamental, segregation and grouping errors), not lab error. Sellers and buyers each sample their own way and get 5-15% differences on Ni, Co and Li. Disputes are settled by splitting the difference or sending to an 'umpire' lab that repeats the same bad sampling. On a $60-150k lot, that swing is $5-15k of pure noise, paid to whoever wins the argument. The industry's chemists treat it like a homogeneous chemical.
solution: Build a containerised, safety-rated sampling and sample-prep station (dryer, rotary divider, splitter, pulverizer, inert handling) and a written ToS-based protocol: incremental sampling from a falling stream or drum auger, particle-size and moisture control, and duplicate-sample bias checks. Send splits to an accredited lab and issue a 'referee certificate' with a stated sampling variance. Provide a two-line settlement clause template that buyer and seller adopt (for example, 'referee result binds') and tie lot IDs to the recycled-content and material-recovery documentation the EU Battery Regulation requires. Extend later to PCB e-waste, catalyst scrap and mixed copper scrap.
why_now: Black mass volumes are ramping with European and US gigafactory ramp-up scrap (often 10-30% early yield loss). EU regulation is pushing black mass toward hazardous-waste treatment and export limits, and Battery Regulation recovery and recycled-content rules are phasing in. Several Western recyclers restructured or were bought out in 2025 (Li-Cycle into Glencore, for example), so sellers now fear counterparty and assay risk. Payables have become the main margin lever as Co and Ni prices swing.
revenue_model: Per-lot referee fee ($1.5-4k) or $15-40 per tonne, annual retainers for large scrap generators, leasing or operating sample-prep stations at recycler gates, and certification and training for recyclers' in-house sampling.
non_obvious_insight: The fight looks like an assay-accuracy problem but it is a sampling problem, and the solution is 1950s-1990s sampling theory that only mining and metallurgy people internalise. Recycling companies are staffed by chemists and process engineers who sample like it is a solution. A person who has been burned by a bad grade-control sample sees the whole market as one giant unsampled stockpile.
first_30_days: Rent time on a commercial sample-prep lab or buy used splitting and pulverizing gear (about $40-60k). Offer a free duplicate-sampling study to three scrap generators or dismantlers: take 10 lots, sample each with the seller's method and yours, and send blind splits to two labs. Show them the between-protocol bias, then sell a 6-month referee retainer. A local mining-lab partner and one senior sampling consultant give instant credibility.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SGS (independent inspection, sampling and assay), Bureau Veritas / Inspectorate (commodities inspection), Intertek (Caleb Brett / minerals and battery testing), Alex Stewart International. White space: Provisional, because the research was severely constrained: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before any search ran, and the direct fetches of incumbent sites returned 403, 404 or no relevant content. Nothing below is web-verified. Likely unserved: (1) A sampling-variance-certified referee product, meaning a Gy/TOS-based protocol with a stated sampling variance, heterogeneity characterisation (variography, sampling nomogram) and a binding-settlement clause. Inspection majors sell 'independent sampling and assay' as a commodity service, but I found no evidence that they publish or guarantee sampling uncertainty for black mass. (2) On-site, containerised, inert-atmosphere sample prep at the recycler or gigafactory gate. Black mass is being pushed toward hazardous-waste treatment in the EU, which makes shipping bulk samples to distant labs harder. (3) Tying lot-level sampling data to EU Battery Regulation material-recovery and recycled-content documentation. The main risk is that SGS, Bureau Veritas/Inspectorate, Intertek or Alex Stewart already offer black-mass sampling and umpire assay and would call this an existing service. The whole wedge depends on their protocols being meaningfully worse than TOS practice, which is unproven and is exactly what the free duplicate-sampling study would test.

title: Bedside Coverage Recovery for Safety-Net Hospitals
one_liner: A pay-on-success desk that helps safety-net hospital financial counselors convert lapsed or presumptively covered patients into full Medicaid within the shrinking retroactive window, with informal-income evidence built over text message, paid a flat fee per approved case by the hospital's revenue cycle budget.
customer: Patient financial services and revenue-cycle leaders, plus hospital presumptive eligibility (HPE) and Medicaid enrollment managers, at safety-net, critical-access and county-owned hospitals in expansion states. Start in Nebraska and adjoining expansion states, where the state hospital association has already campaigned against retroactive-coverage cuts. The enrollee pays nothing. The hospital pays only when a case is approved.
problem: Two hospital-side facts changed. First, starting January 1, 2027, retroactive Medicaid coverage for expansion adults shrinks to one month before the application month (per Justice in Aging and other H.R. 1 explainers), so every day a lapsed patient waits to reapply can turn a billable encounter into charity care. Second, HPE screens for the work requirement by attestation and gives up to 60 days of temporary coverage, after which the patient needs a full determination, and hospitals are being urged to build conversion assistance. Projections cited by Applied Policy put FY2027 coverage losses at 2.3M, with about 43% procedural. The hospital sees the loss first: an inactive eligibility response at registration or the ED desk. But the counselor's usual application flow stalls on cash, gig and informal workers, who cannot produce payroll or wage records. The hospital eats the bill. (Assumption to verify: existing hospital Medicaid-eligibility outsourcers handle standard applications but not informal-income compliance evidence.)
solution: A Coverage Recovery Desk delivered as a light workflow, not an EHR integration. (1) Daily feed: a CSV or SFTP list of registrations with inactive or self-pay coverage and prior Medicaid, plus HPE patients at day 20 of 60. (2) Outreach in hours: hospital-branded SMS or WhatsApp in the patient's language. (3) Evidence build: the attestation and receipt engine from the sibling Cure Desk, with third-party attestations for cash workers. Patients who have a bank or payroll trail are routed to the state's own Emmy or SteadyIQ flow. Exemption triage and any state-optional excused months for inpatient stays are documented. (4) Retro-clock calculator: maps each open encounter to the one retroactive month and tells the counselor which filing date protects which claims. This is the hospital-specific feature, and the first thing they will use daily. (5) Counselor submits with a complete packet; we never decide eligibility. (6) Dashboard: dollars of self-pay converted to Medicaid-billable, by lapse reason. Digital-trail patients cost us almost nothing, so margin comes from doing the cash residual efficiently.
why_now: Jan 1, 2027 combines the work requirement, six-month renewals for expansion adults, and the retroactive-coverage cut, all landing on the hospital revenue cycle at once. Uncompensated care is already implicated in rural hospital closures. Hospitals are being told to strengthen HPE-to-full-Medicaid conversion assistance now. Cheap messaging, OCR and translation mean a counselor can handle several times more cases per day than with paper and phone tag.
revenue_model: Pay-on-success, no software fee to start: a flat $150-300 per approved reinstatement or HPE-to-full conversion, tiered by encounter dollars at stake. A flat fee per approval, not a percentage of Medicaid collections, because Medicaid billing-agent payment rules generally restrict percentage-of-collections arrangements (counsel to confirm). Optional $2-4k per month CFO analytics tier (self-pay at risk by lapse reason, retro-window leakage). Illustrative unit economics (assumptions to validate in the audit): a 150-bed hospital sees 120 lapse-related self-pay encounters a month, 25% are reinstated at $200, giving $6k a month or $72k a year per hospital, versus a Medicaid-paid stay worth thousands. 30 hospitals is about $2.2M ARR. Later: subcontract informal-income packets to incumbent eligibility outsourcers.
non_obvious_insight: The hospital registration desk is the earliest reliable detector of work-requirement and procedural terminations, because an eligibility check runs at every visit. Plans learn from monthly files, and states rely on notices that cash workers miss. It is also the moment of maximum patient motivation, with the bill in hand. Plans are limited to a supporting role under the IFR and MCO procurement is slow, but hospitals are neither plans nor determiners, and their counselors already file Medicaid applications every day. The cash-flow logic is lopsided: a $200 fee against a stay Medicaid may pay thousands for, and the one-month retro window makes speed a priced variable for the first time.
first_30_days: Send 15 Nebraska and regional revenue-cycle leaders a free 'lapse leakage audit': they share a de-identified 90-day list of self-pay encounters with prior Medicaid, and we estimate dollars at risk and how many are informal-income cases (procedural lapses today stand in for work-requirement lapses). Sign a BAA and a pay-on-success pilot with the first one or two. Run 20-25 live cases by hand: the counselor works from our SMS templates and packet PDF, and we track time to filing, approvals and the encounters saved by the retro-clock calculator. In parallel, ask the state Medicaid agency and a hospital association contact how reinstatement, reapplication and HPE conversion work for noncompliance terminations, and get counsel's sign-off on the fee structure.
lineage: mutation of I0573 ('Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CMS Emmy (Eligibility Made Easy) app and Emmy API, SteadyIQ (Income Passport / Verification Hub), Digital Public Works, Maximus, Optum, Acentra, Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, Curam/Merative (state-side community engagement modules). White space: Nobody I found sells an enrollee-side monthly ledger to MCOs or FQHCs that ingests bank, gig and pay-stub data, computes $580 or 80 hours against a state's look-back rules, and produces a state-specific 30-day cure packet. Nothing turned up in searches, CMS vendor pledges or CBPP/KFF/Georgetown landscape coverage. Vendors sit on either side of that gap. State-side vendors (SteadyIQ, Emmy, Maximus, Optum, Deloitte) sell to state agencies. Provider and plan-side vendors (Pointcare, Findhelp, mPulse) sell eligibility monitoring and outreach without gig-income packet building. The clearest unserved segment is workers with no digital trail: cash, informal and 1099-below-threshold workers such as day labor, cleaning and landscaping. Consent-based verification (CBV) via payroll, bank or gig platforms cannot reach them. The 30-day cure step, meaning a compiled packet after a noncompliance notice, is also not addressed by any product I found. The wedge is narrow and could close quickly. States with CBV (SteadyIQ, Emmy) let the enrollee connect accounts directly, which makes a separate packet redundant there. MCOs may be poor buyers because the IFR bars plans from determining compliance and gives them only a supporting role. Pointcare and Findhelp already own the FQHC and MCO relationships and could add a module. Research limits: my web search budget ran out after four searches, so I relied on page fetches. I could not load the CBPP vendor landscape, the Health Affairs piece or the Federal Register text (all blocked), and I could not confirm what Propel for Plans does or any vendor's funding. | How this version avoids them: Pointcare sells lapse detection and retention to FQHCs before claims reject, while this sells recovery and conversion to hospital revenue cycle after lapse, with a different buyer, trigger and pricing. Findhelp sells eligibility-at-risk flags to plans, states and CBOs. mPulse and Propel do outreach and notices. None of them builds informal-income evidence or the retro-clock, and none prices on a hospital's approved case. SteadyIQ, Emmy, and the state-side vendor pledges serve states, and digital-trail patients are handed to them. The cash and informal residue they cannot reach is the only part we do. The buyer is not an MCO, which removes the IFR supporting-role restriction and slow plan procurement. New risk not covered by the parent's research: existing hospital eligibility outsourcers. Mitigate by offering our packet builder as their informal-income subcontractor and by staying on the pay-on-success pricing they already understand.

title: Agency E&O Insurers Fund AI-Exclusion File Reviews
one_liner: The insurers and endorsed programs that cover insurance agencies pay to put an AI-exclusion review and a client-acknowledgment file behind every commercial renewal their insured agencies handle. It is funded as loss control, in the way cyber insurers fund security scans, and the agency pays little or nothing.
customer: Payer: underwriting and program managers at insurance-agency E&O carriers and MGAs, and the state independent-agent associations that endorse an E&O program to their members. Users: the insured agencies with 5-100 staff. Buyer chain: the party who bears the cost of failure-to-warn claims pays, and the party who does the work receives the tool.
problem: Agency E&O carriers will pay defence costs and settlements when a client discovers, after an AI-caused loss, that the renewal quietly excluded AI and nobody told them. The exclusions are silent (the premium barely changes), they arrive in mass on 1/1/2027 renewals, and the claims will surface in 2027-2029. Even where the duty to advise is weak, defence costs are incurred anyway. Today these carriers have only PDF advisories and webinars, no data on whether any insured agency did anything, and no view of aggregate exposure across their book.
solution: A white-labelled program, called the 'Exclusion File' in the carrier's brand, with three parts. (1) Agency workflow: the agency forwards the renewal quote or policy PDF and receives the diff, the breadth score and a gap letter. The client e-signs an acknowledgment, either accepting the exclusion or asking for affirmative cover or a negotiated carve-back. Everything is stored in an audit-ready vault, which is the classic E&O defence of documented advice. (2) Carrier dashboard: the share of insured agencies enrolled, the share of commercial renewals reviewed, unresolved acknowledgments, and anonymised aggregate exclusion prevalence and breadth by line and by carrier form. It shows the carrier's own exposure. (3) Underwriting hook: a supplemental question on the E&O application, 'Do you review renewals for AI exclusions and retain client acknowledgments?', and an optional rate credit or deductible break for agencies that complete the program on 90% or more of their commercial renewals. The diff engine underneath is the same as in the sharpened offspring, so the marginal build cost is the vault, the e-sign flow and the dashboard.
why_now: The first large exclusion cycle is 1 Jan 2027, so an E&O carrier that acts in Q4 2026 has a defensible risk-control story before any claims exist. Trade and association content already urges agencies to review renewals (Big I on the Verisk rollout, Agents United, IA Magazine on 9 Sep 2026), so the carriers' insureds are being asked to act with no help. Cyber insurers that fund scans and security tooling for insureds have made the loss-control-for-premium-credit model familiar to underwriters. Agency E&O is a concentrated market with few carriers and programs, so a small number of decisions covers a lot of insured agencies.
revenue_model: The carrier or program pays $600-1,500 per enrolled agency per year, plus $25-60k per year for a quarterly AI-exclusion exposure report for its underwriters and reinsurers. The agency pays a $49-99 copay per diff, or nothing where the carrier sponsors it fully. An association that endorses the program takes an endorsed-vendor fee of 10-15% of agency revenue, which is how associations already monetise vendor programs. As an illustration: a carrier insuring 1,500 agencies, 20% enrolled at $900 each, is about $270k a year, plus the data subscription. These figures are estimates to be tested in pilot.
non_obvious_insight: The E&O insurer is the only party in the chain that pays whether or not a court finds a duty to advise, so it does not care about the legal debate that weakens the broker-side pitch. The distribution lever is also the E&O application. Once the supplemental question is on the form, agencies need a compliant answer every year, and this program becomes the standard way to give one. The same carrier-funded logic scales to the next silent-exclusion wave, whether PFAS, cyber war, biometric or another, so the customer can renew and expand on the same integration.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: write a 2-page memo for underwriters with three concrete failure-to-warn fact patterns on 1/1/2027 renewals and a list of the largest agency E&O carriers, MGAs and association-endorsed programs. Book calls through LinkedIn and state association staff, and aim for 5 calls. Days 10-25: offer 3 state associations a free 45-minute webinar, 'AI exclusions on your Jan 1 renewals', which is a cheap way to capture 100+ agencies. Sign 10-25 of them as a pilot cohort using the concierge diff. Days 20-30: take the pilot cohort's hit-rate numbers (how many renewals had a new AI exclusion the agency had not flagged) back to the carriers and associations as a pilot pitch. Ask for a 3-month pilot at about $15k for 25 agencies, or an association endorsement. Carrier cycles run 3-6 months, so the association route generates the first revenue.
lineage: mutation of I1133 ('Renewal Radar for Silent AI Exclusions'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Patra (AI Policy Checking), Quandri, Zywave Apex / Advisor Agent, Testudo. White space: A real gap remains, but it is much narrower than the pitch. Nobody found sells a commercial-lines, broker-facing workflow that (1) takes a book's actual renewal forms schedules, quotes and binders (not just carrier-level filings), (2) detects and normalises AI exclusion breadth for each client, including bespoke wording such as Berkley PC 51380 and unnamed 'AI' language, (3) ties it to a 90-day renewal calendar, and (4) hands the producer a client-ready gap letter and a matched affirmative placement. Pieces exist separately. Patra reads commercial policies for hidden exclusions but is not AI-specific. Quandri and Zywave own the 90-day renewal trigger but show no exclusion-level AI flagging. Testudo and Armilla offer AI-use mapping and placement but only for their own paper.

Three parts of the plan are weak. (a) The SERFF scraper and exclusion database are not a moat. Trades Coverage already compiled 4,078 records for free. Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs and ShadowLock publish free trackers, and Certian even ships CC BY 4.0 CSV and JSON. (b) A filing shows a carrier adopted a form in a state. It does not show the form is attached to client X's policy, so the real signal is the policy document, not the filing. (c) SERFF filing access covers admitted markets only. Surplus lines is where most E&O, D&O and tech-E&O AI exclusions sit, and it is largely invisible to SERFF.

Wedge that looks unserved: commercial professional-liability and tech-E&O accounts (design firms, law, accounting, software, agencies) where exclusions are broadest and most bespoke, for independent agencies without an in-house risk-advisory team, priced as a renewal-review add-on rather than a filings database. | How this version avoids them: Zywave, Quandri, Patra, Rosella and FurtherAI all sell productivity software or outsourcing to agencies, and none produces carrier-visible compliance evidence, an acknowledgment vault or a book-level exposure dashboard. Testudo, Armilla, AIUC, Mount and Munich Re/Mosaic sell AI liability cover and court brokers to sell it, which makes them conflicted advisers for an E&O insurer. This is neutral and earns no placement commission. The free trackers (Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs, ShadowLock, Trades Coverage) are content marketing and do not produce a per-client acknowledgment record. Their data is a free input here. The real competitor is the carrier's current PDF advisory and webinar, which is non-consumption of any real workflow. SERFF vendors (InsuranceFiling, Filing360, FilingRamp) sell to compliance teams, and I found nobody selling to agency-E&O underwriters.

title: Continuity Retainer for One-Licensee Funeral Homes
one_liner: Key-person insurance for funeral homes: a bench of pre-credentialed licensed directors and embalmers who step in within 24-48 hours when the owner is sick, burned out or gone, with a built-in path to succession.
customer: Independent and rural funeral homes with one or two licensed staff (roughly 30-150 calls a year), typically owner-operators aged 55-75. A second buyer is the family of an owner who has died or fallen ill and needs the home kept legal while it is sold.
problem: States require a licensed funeral director or manager-in-charge, and often a licensed embalmer, for an establishment to operate. The owner is on call 24/7/365 and hasn't had a real week off in years. One heart attack, surgery or burnout means the home cannot legally operate, families get funneled to the consolidator down the road, and a business built over three generations is sold at a distressed price. Informal 'relief director' phone lists exist, but there is no bench, no contract, no reciprocity or board paperwork handled, and no guarantee anyone answers at 3 a.m.
solution: Recruit retired and semi-retired licensed directors and embalmers, including many leaving consolidators, and pre-credential them in a target state cluster with background checks and reciprocity filings. Sell continuity retainers that guarantee a set number of coverage days a year (real vacations, weekends off) plus emergency activation within 24-48 hours at a day rate. The company handles the state-board notice of interim manager changes. A succession track lets an interim operator or next-generation licensed buyer convert into a partner or buyer with seller financing, so owners have an alternative to a roll-up.
why_now: Consolidation keeps shrinking the independent pool (SCI alone bought about 22 funeral homes and 2 cemeteries for roughly $101M in 2025). The licensed workforce is aging while mortuary-school pipelines are thin. Rising cremation lowers revenue per case, making full-time second hires unaffordable for small homes. Rural closures are creating 'funeral deserts'. Many states have passed occupational-license recognition laws that make multi-state relief staffing easier.
revenue_model: Retainer of $900-$2,000/month per home including N coverage days. Activation day rate of $800-$1,400 billed to the home, with a 25-30% margin over what the licensee is paid. Per-case fees for trade embalming and prep-room services. A 1-2% success fee on succession transactions.
non_obvious_insight: The real asset of an independent funeral home isn't the building, it's one license holder with a phone, and that is a single point of failure. Consolidators know it and wait. Owners will pay to sleep: this is a wellness and continuity product disguised as staffing, and its best feature is the succession pipeline it creates once a trusted operator is already inside the home.
first_30_days: Recruit eight retired licensed directors and embalmers through state association chapters and retiree groups. Check each state board's rules for temporary manager-in-charge designation. Pitch 20 one-licensee homes in two adjacent counties at a $1,200/month founding rate with a 'test weekend off' guarantee. Sign the first three, and run the first covered weekend within 30 days to produce a testimonial.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: NFDA Funeral Career Hub and NFDA recruiting services, NFDA succession planning member resources and SESCO HR consulting, Selected Independent Funeral Homes (staff recruitment and Selected Transfer Services), American Mortuary Service (trade embalming and removals, Dallas/Fort Worth). White space: Caveat first: this verdict has low-to-moderate confidence. The WebSearch budget for the session was already exhausted (200 of 200), so none of the planned 6-12 searches ran. I did not use WebFetch on a search engine to get around the limit. All I did was fetch about 15 specific vendor and industry URLs. Most guessed domains did not resolve, and the ones that resolved were adjacent players, not direct competitors. "No direct competitor found" therefore means "not found with a very limited method", not "verified absent".

What the limited evidence supports as unserved: (1) A contracted, pre-credentialed, multi-state bench with a guaranteed activation SLA. The only related products I could confirm are a job board (NFDA), an association recruiting and transfer program (Selected), trade embalming vendors (American Mortuary Service) and member-only succession content (NFDA). None of them takes on the license-holder single point of failure. (2) The bundled path from interim operator to succession buyer with seller financing. I found nobody offering it, and it is the strongest differentiator because it turns a cost centre into a deal pipeline.

Risks I could not verify and that could still kill or reshape the idea, all of which come from the idea file and general reasoning, not from research:
- State law. Many boards tie the establishment license to a named manager-in-charge who must be there full-time or on premises, and some have short or no temporary-designation windows. If temporary designation is unavailable in the target states, the 24-48 hour activation promise fails legally. Check this first, state by state.
- Adverse selection and price. $10.8k-24k a year is roughly 2-8% of revenue for a home doing 30-150 calls, and a retainer is bought mostly by owners who feel at risk.
- Liability, insurance and non-solicit exposure when a stranger runs someone else's establishment.
- Supply. A bench of eight retirees has to be dense enough to reach homes in rural counties within 24 hours, so density in one cluster matters more than breadth.

title: Fifteen-Minute Court Reporting for Family Law Hearings
one_liner: Remove the half-day minimum by dispatching remote stenographers into many short hearings per day, so a family-law litigant gets a certified record of a 15-minute hearing for about $100.
customer: California family law and probate attorneys and solo practitioners. Self-represented litigants reached through DV legal aid organizations and family law facilitators. Legal aid groups buying bulk credits. Later, county courts contracting to meet the new duty to provide records to indigent litigants.
problem: California logged roughly 3 million civil, family and probate hearings without a verbatim record between April 2023 and March 2026, about 7 in 10. Without a record, appeals of custody and restraining-order rulings fail, because the appellant cannot show error. Private reporters charge $250-$500+ appearance minimums, since a reporter can wait 2-3 hours for a 12-minute calendar item. Nobody pays that for a routine hearing. In 2026 the California Supreme Court (Family Violence Appellate Project v. Superior Court) held that courts must give indigent litigants an official verbatim record on request, and courts do not have the reporters to comply.
solution: A dispatch platform that reads court calendars, predicts when each matter will be called from historical hearing-type durations per department, and pages a remote reporter into the court's Zoom or Teams feed only for the minutes needed. One reporter covers 8-12 short hearings a day across departments. Deliver a certified transcript in 24-72 hours, with an AI first draft for the reporter to scope. Price is a flat $95 for hearings up to 15 minutes and about $8 per page beyond that. Start where remote appearance and remote reporting are allowed (California's AB 3013 authorizes remote reporting, and each court's procedures need checking). Pitch courts on per-department-day capacity at a discount to staffing a full-time reporter.
why_now: The 2026 California Supreme Court ruling creates a legal duty courts cannot currently meet. AB 3013 (2024) opened remote reporting. The workforce is projected to be about 5,500 reporters short by 2030. Family courts are widely on video. Reporter dead time is a scheduling problem that software can solve.
revenue_model: Per-hearing fees paid by attorneys and litigants. Bulk credits funded by legal aid and foundation grants. Later B2G contracts priced per courtroom-day. The reporter keeps about 55-60% of each hearing fee, which beats their typical hourly yield because dead time is eliminated.
non_obvious_insight: The reporter shortage is partly a utilization problem. In a busy family calendar department, a reporter may write 2-3 hours of a 7-hour day and wait the rest. Remote hopping sells that dead time to several litigants at once, so the price can fall 70% while the reporter earns more.
first_30_days: Sign 3-5 remote-capable freelance or semi-retired reporters. Pick one county whose family departments run on Zoom and cover it manually with a shared spreadsheet and a text pager. Offer 10 solo family law attorneys and two DV appellate nonprofits (start with the Family Violence Appellate Project) at-cost coverage of their next 5 hearings. Track wait time per hearing so the prediction model has real data.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Steno (Steno Agency Inc.), DirectDep, StenoScout, Incumbent agencies (Veritext, Esquire, Combs Reporting, Coalition Court Reporters). White space: Nobody offers flat-fee coverage of 15-minute California family-law hearings. That is because the core mechanic, private reporters dialing in from anywhere, is currently barred. Gov. Code 69959 says 'Remote court reporting shall not be used by courts to make the record of any court proceedings' and defines it as a stenographer not present in the courtroom (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959/). The only exception, Gov. Code 69959.5, allows remote reporting only by 'full-time official reporters ... employed by the participating superior court', physically in a court facility, in 13 pilot counties, capped at 10-20% of reporters (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959-5/). San Diego's court page states 'the court is prohibited by law from allowing remote court reporting for any court proceeding' (https://sdcourt.ca.gov/sdcourt/generalinformation/resourcelists/courtreporterinformation). The idea's claim that AB 3013 'opened remote reporting' to a private platform is wrong. Unserved and still legal: (1) physical-presence short-hearing coverage, where one pro tem covers several departments in the same courthouse using calendar-based duration prediction, and no vendor markets a per-hearing SKU; (2) a scheduling and utilization layer sold to courts to fill pro tem and official reporter slots, aimed at hiring and retention (the ruling names 'pro tem reporters paid by the court' as a compliance route, and court reporter counsel is calling on courts to lift hiring freezes); (3) fast certified transcripts of court electronic recordings for attorneys who need appellate-grade records. The white space is real but is a legal-regime bet on remote reporting being opened to private reporters, plus a narrow physical-hopping wedge. It is not a software-only wedge. Court reporter unions opposed AB 3013 and are a political headwind.

title: Load-Proven Warranty Wrap for Data Halls
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of chasing OEMs for owners as warranties expire, run a standardized load-proof test before expiry, fix what the OEM owes for free, then sell a capacity-backed warranty wrap that covers the post-expiry tail, priced from a proprietary fleet failure database.
customer: First buyers: owners and lenders' technical advisors of energized data halls approaching OEM warranty expiry, asking for a standardized Load-Proven test and certificate (a covenant-friendly document for refinancing or ABS). Later buyers: the same owners buying multi-year coverage for gensets, UPS, chillers and liquid-cooling CDUs. The capacity provider (a specialty insurer or reinsurer) is a third party in the money flow.
problem: The parent's contingency model is hard to collect and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds. Behind that is a bigger issue: once OEM warranties lapse, owners of AI halls with dense power and liquid cooling carry an unpriced failure tail, and nobody has independent load-tested failure data on these systems. OEM service contracts cover a single vendor's gear and are priced generically. Lenders financing GPU-era assets see equipment residual risk with no standard way to test or rate it.
solution: Phase 1, within 6 months: sell a standardized Load-Proven protocol. It is a 3-5 day staged load test (gensets, UPS and battery, chillers and CDUs, breakers), thermography, oil, coolant and battery diagnostics, using a load-bank rental partner and NETA-type testing subcontractors. Each test outputs a certificate and, where a defect shows, an OEM claim package while the OEM is still liable. Every test feeds a proprietary failure and degradation database. Phase 2, months 6-18: place multi-year tail coverage for tested gear through a broker or MGA partner on a quota-share basis with an insurer or reinsurer. Only gear that passed the test is bound. Defects surfaced by the test are repaired at the OEM's cost first, so the wrap covers a cleaner tail. Phase 3: become the MGA, and push the test protocol into loan covenants and insurer schedules as the standard.
why_now: AI halls introduce liquid-cooling and high-density power gear with immature public failure data, so generic pricing is either too expensive or blind. Data center lending and ABS need equipment-condition standards. Phase slippage means a large group of halls will pass through OEM expiry without ever having been stressed. Cheap LLM extraction of test logs and maintenance records lets a small team standardize reports across sites.
revenue_model: Phase 1: $60-120K per hall for the Load-Proven test (much of it load-bank pass-through), plus any claim-based fee. Phase 2: broker commission, then MGA ceding and profit commission on premium. non_obvious_insight: The inspection is both the revenue product and the underwriting filter, and the two feed each other. Defects found pre-expiry are paid by the OEM, which reduces adverse selection, and the resulting data is a cornered resource: independent, fleet-level, load-based, across OEMs. The parent treated the warranty as an asset to recover. Goal: one paid pilot test signed and one written indication of appetite from a capacity provider.

title: Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that finds and files the warranty claims on energized-but-empty data halls before OEM warranty clocks silently expire.
customer: Colocation developers, powered-shell landlords, neocloud operators and enterprise owners with phased or delayed-tenant builds, especially those with halls commissioned 6-14 months ago and not yet loaded. The owner pays a percentage of recovered value, plus an optional per-asset tracking subscription.
problem: Warranty clocks on generators, UPS systems, chillers, CRAH/CDUs, switchgear, and batteries usually start at shipment or startup, not when a tenant loads the hall. With delayed leases and mid-build AI redesigns, halls sit energized and idle for months. Many defects only show under real load (UPS capacitors, chiller compressors, wet-stacking gensets, breaker trip curves, coolant chemistry). By the time the tenant ramps, the warranty has expired. The turnover package is 50,000+ pages of PDFs that ops never reads, the punch-list deferrals are lost, and OEM maintenance records required to keep coverage valid are often missing. Nobody owns the clock.
solution: Ingest POs, OEM warranty terms, startup sheets, Cx reports, shipping documents and maintenance logs with an LLM pipeline to build a serial-number-level warranty ledger with real expiry dates and voiding conditions. Flag anything expiring within 120 days. Run a targeted load-dependent-defect inspection before expiry (thermography, oil and coolant samples, capacitor and battery checks, breaker testing). File claims, negotiate warranty start-date deferrals or extensions with the OEM while leverage still exists, and fix missing maintenance-record gaps. For new builds, sell a PO-stage clause pack that defers warranty start to beneficial occupancy.
why_now: There is a glut of speculative shells and delayed tenant handoffs. Reporting in 2026 shows close to half of planned US builds slipping, with only about a third of 2026 target capacity under active construction. That means many halls are powered, commissioned and idle. Equipment was bought at peak prices with tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. LLMs can now read messy closeout binders cheaply, which was the labor bottleneck for audits like this.
revenue_model: 25-30% of recovered value or avoided cost on claims and negotiated extensions, no fee if nothing is recovered. Optional $150-400 per asset per year tracking subscription. $15K-40K fixed-fee closeout audits for owners who want certainty. PO-stage clause-pack consulting for developers.
non_obvious_insight: The warranty is the only major asset on a data center balance sheet that expires silently. OEMs will defer warranty start dates at PO time, but almost no one negotiates it because the project team is fighting for delivery slots, not paperwork. After the fact, the owner's ops team inherits the docs with no idea when the clocks started. The money is in the punch-list items that were 'to be fixed later' and the load-dependent defects that only appear after the hall is finally used.

Deliver a 'expiring within 90 days' hit list and file the first claims before the first invoice.

title: Notarized Mitigation Records: The Evidence Standard for Wildfire Credits
one_liner: A score-agnostic verification layer where contractors capture signed photos that are cross-checked against imagery and issued as portable machine-readable Verified Mitigation Records, which carriers and certifiers accept.
customer: First, Front Range defensible-space crews, roofers, ember-vent installers and drone inspectors, who pay per job. Then wildfire certification programs (Wildfire Partners, IBHS-style programs) that pay per avoided inspection. Then carriers' appeal desks and underwriters, who read the record through a free API and later pay for ingestion. HOAs and fire-safe councils are the bulk channel.
problem: Homeowners spend $5k-$30k hardening a house and cannot prove it in a way an insurer will accept. Photos and photo-log templates are easy to fake, and AI image generation makes unverified photos worth less each year. HB25-1182 obliges insurers to credit documented mitigation but sets no evidence standard, and on-site inspection capacity is the bottleneck. Contractors cannot promise an insurance credit, so hardening jobs stay unsold.
solution: A web app (PWA first) for contractors and homeowners with guided capture: a checklist of shots for Zone 0/1/2, vents, roof and gutters, taken with signed capture (C2PA-style content credentials, device attestation, GPS, time and heading). The system cross-checks each claim against archived and new imagery and lidar, for example that vegetation was cleared between two dated images or that a roof is Class A. It issues a Verified Mitigation Record as an open-schema JSON file plus a PDF, versioned and portable across carriers. The schema is published under an open licence and co-developed with a fire-safe council. Carrier and certifier readers are free, and acceptance outcomes feed a per-carrier acceptance dataset. The capture layer would use an existing signed-capture SDK, not a new one.
why_now: Generative image tools have made unverified photo evidence untrustworthy. Signed-capture standards and SDKs are now commodity. HB25-1182 turned documented mitigation into a legal object with no format. High-resolution archives and public lidar are cheap enough to act as the independent witness. This is also the inversion of the parent idea: instead of proving a model wrong about the house, prove the house right and let any score-maker read it.
revenue_model: $49-$89 per notarized job, paid by the contractor and passed through in the quote. $40-$120 per avoided on-site reinspection from certification programs. $15-$60 per accepted record from carriers via subscription or API. Agents from a rebuttal desk buy per file. At 300 contractors doing 40 records a year at $65, that is about $0.8M, and the carrier and certifier layers scale it much further.
non_obvious_insight: The reason insurers can decline third-party imagery is that they cannot trust or parse it, not that they are hostile. Give them evidence with provenance, in a schema they can auto-ingest, and the cost of handling an appeal falls. The parent's moat, the concession database, then extends into a network: contractors, homeowners and carriers all gain from a shared format, as with ACORD forms or the Uniform Appraisal Dataset. Because the layer describes the house and not the score, it holds up when Zesty, Cotality or Verisk change their models, and it is neutral in a way a scorer can never be.
first_30_days: Sign 5 Boulder and Jefferson County defensible-space and roofing contractors on a free pilot. Ship the guided-capture PWA with the imagery cross-check. Notarize 60 real jobs. Ask 3 agencies to submit those records in real credit requests and log carrier responses. Propose a 10-file remote pre-verification pilot to Wildfire Partners. Publish schema v0.1 on GitHub.
