title: Recall Drills: State QC Findings Become Worker Training
one_liner: A recall-notice system for SNAP errors: every finding from a state's own QC review and every H.R.1 rule change becomes a dollar-tagged synthetic drill within 14 days, delivered through the state's CQI field staff to new hires in its highest-error counties, with an audit trail for corrective-action plans.
customer: Wedge: North Carolina's SNAP continuous-quality-improvement (CQI) unit. Its staff are former county workers who visit each of the 100 county departments monthly, plus the counties the state has already flagged as high-error. NC's 6.69% rate sits 0.69 points above the 6% cliff, and the parent research puts crossing it at about $140M a year. Payer: the state SNAP director's training/CQI line. Users: CQI specialists and county supervisors. Next states: Louisiana (7.61%) and any state within about 1.5 points of a 6/8/10% tier line.
problem: QC findings reach workers months after the case action, as webinars and memos. H.R.1 rule churn (work-requirement, noncitizen and utility-allowance changes) creates fresh errors faster than classroom training absorbs them. New hires learn on live caseloads, and Kansas cites turnover as an error driver. Counties are told 'documenting, documenting, documenting' but have no per-worker evidence trail. A handful of CQI staff cannot be in 100 counties every day.
solution: Three pieces. (1) An error-to-drill pipeline: CQI staff upload a QC finding at element level (stacked shelter deduction after a rent change, biweekly pay-stub conversion, household member who left). Within 14 days we return a synthetic twin case, scored with PolicyEngine as the oracle and hand-checked against the state manual, and push it to the assigned counties. (2) A 30-day new-hire certification track over the top three error elements, with pre/post scores and time-to-competency. (3) A CQI console with per-county and per-worker error-type heatmaps and a one-click 'CAP evidence packet' PDF (assigned, completed, score trend) that counties attach to corrective-action documentation. Drills test the input and verification decisions workers actually make (what to verify, which income to budget, which old entry to close), not the arithmetic the eligibility system already does.
why_now: The FY2027 QC sample year opens Oct 1, 2026. It is the first year measured under the new rules and it sets the FY2030 cost share (FY2029 and later use the rate from three fiscal years earlier). FY2028 exposure is effectively locked to the state's better of FY2025 or FY2026, so the next lever is FY2027 onward. The 75% state/local admin cost share also starts Oct 1, 2026. USDA published FY2025 rates on June 24, 2026: 41 states are above 6% and the national rate is 10.62%, and states above 6% must file remediation plans. States are visibly buying: Alabama DHR posted a QC assessment and training RFP, and NC's one-click 'close old deduction' prompt has been used more than 20,000 times, which shows targeted micro-interventions get adopted.
revenue_model: Year-1 state pilot of $60-90k for 12-15 named counties (verify it sits under each state's small-purchase limit). This expands to statewide at $250-400k a year. Counties outside the state contract pay $150-300 per worker, and new-hire certification is $250 per hire. All prices are unvalidated, so get the budget line from the CQI director before writing case #13. Realistic ceiling is about $10-20M ARR across the roughly 40 states above the threshold, so this is the modest-ceiling, fast-to-cash version.
non_obvious_insight: The product is closing the lag, not teaching skill. States already hold the scarcest asset, their own QC findings, and lose months turning it into training. A recall loop (finding, twin drill, completion evidence) cannot be copied by a vendor that only has the generic USDA taxonomy. It is one data-sharing MOU with a state QC unit away, and US Digital Response reports such agreements take 3 weeks to 3 months. Pick the launch state by distance to a cliff times benefit dollars, not by pain: NY at 13% needs a 3-point cut just to reach the 10% tier, while NC at 6.69% can plausibly cross 6%. A 0%-error county is still charged for the state average, so the state CQI unit, not the county, is the customer.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: 20 calls with NC CQI staff, county DSS directors and the state county association, asking who owns a budget line for this and what the last training tool cost. Days 5-15: build 12 drills from public sources only (H.R.1 rule changes, the publicly described stacked-shelter-deduction failure, biweekly wage conversion, household-member removal), and script the 14-day finding-to-drill workflow. Days 15-25: run a 3-county new-hire pre/post pilot with CQI staff as co-facilitators. Days 25-30: hand the state a CAP evidence packet sample and a one-page letter of intent with a price, and ask the CQI director to name the budget line.

title: Dark Roof Capital: Buy, Cure, Re-Perform
one_liner: Invert the parent. Instead of being paid a $3k fee to cure other people's stranded solar loans, buy those loans at dark-roof prices, finish the systems with a proprietary per-AHJ cure playbook, and keep the full value uplift as a re-performing loan pool.
customer: Sellers: credit unions, banks, servicers and ABS trusts or controlling-class holders that want dark and forbearance-stuck solar loans off their books. Capital side: distressed-credit funds, family offices and NPL buyers who want a new niche but cannot cure a roof. Homeowners are offered a cure and a payment reset in exchange for reinstating payments.
problem: Dark solar loans are an orphan asset class with broken pricing. NPL desks discount them to zero collateral value because they cannot fix the system. Lenders will not cure at scale and cannot collect on a roof that produces nothing. A cure costs perhaps 10-15% of the loan balance yet restores most of its value, but a $3k cure fee captures only about 10% of the $20k+ of value created. The holder of the loan keeps 90%, and today nobody who can cure holds the loan.
solution: Use the forensic pack from the parent as an underwriting engine. Sell a Bid Desk: audit a seller's dark loans, then quote a purchase price within 10 days. First 6 months: sell a zero-upfront cure-share product to a credit union (we finish the jobs, and take about 25% of restored loan value once PTO is achieved and payments resume), funded by a small working-capital line. Then buy pools through an SPV with a licensed sub-servicer. Cure with the playbook and offer borrowers a reset (a rate or principal modification in exchange for reinstatement). Hold or resell re-performing pools. Longer term, securitize re-performing solar loans, as mortgage RPL funds do. Purchases are limited to loans where the borrower is engaged and in forbearance, with reps and warranties and a seller-funded holdback for claims.
why_now: Freedom Forever, Sunnova, SunPower and PosiGen mean a growing pool of dark loans now exists, with forbearance windows expiring. Post-25D, lenders are shifting from origination to workout and want clean books. Mortgage NPL and RPL buyers already exist and are looking for new asset classes in a higher-rate world. Cheap agentic records recovery makes the per-loan diligence cost low enough to bid on small-balance loans.
revenue_model: Phase 1 (0-6 months): cure-share, about 25% of restored loan value, with zero upfront cost to the seller. Phase 2: spread on purchased loans. Illustration only: buy a $35k loan at about $11k (roughly 32% of balance), spend about $3.5k to cure, and a re-performing loan is worth about $24-28k, giving a $10-13k gross uplift before servicing, legal and default haircuts. Investors in the SPV pay roughly a 1.5% management fee and 20% carry above an 8% preferred return. The operating company also earns cure and coordination fees. Phase 3: RPL securitization fees.
non_obvious_insight: Fee-for-service captures the wrong slice of value, and whoever can cure at the lowest cost can bid the highest and still make money. Pure NPL funds cannot cure, lenders will not, and cure contractors have no balance sheet, so the buyer with the best per-AHJ playbook has a structural cost advantage. Dark solar loans also carry a specific hidden liability for buyers. Under the FTC Holder Rule, a homeowner can raise installer misconduct claims against whoever holds the loan. Curing the system removes the basis for most of those claims, so the cure is also the de-risking step, and buyers who cannot cure are pricing that risk at its maximum.
first_30_days: Use the audit engine to build a bid model on 50-100 loans from a friendly credit union or servicer under NDA, and price them. Get a commitment letter from one distressed-credit family office for a $1-2M first-loss pilot. Commission a legal memo on the Holder Rule, state lender and servicer licensing, and rescission risk, and identify a licensed sub-servicer. Sign one cure-share deal (no purchase) covering about 30 loans to measure real cure cost per tier and how many borrowers reinstate. Write a one-page pool teaser for investors. The riskiest assumption is borrower willingness to resume payments and rescission exposure, so measure reinstatement rates before buying anything.

The seven Freedom Forever financiers have ops teams, and Sunrun and GoodLeap have crews. Solar Servicing LLC (which took over Mosaic's servicing), credit unions, bank holders and ABS investors have no step-in playbook. I found no completion vendor aimed at them. (3) Legacy stranded books. Titan (an estimated 150,000 households), SunPower, Sunnova, PosiGen, Mosaic-financed loans and others. Lenders may not know which loans sit on de-energized systems, so an identify-then-cure offer has little competition. The stay-relief order dates to about August 2026, so the seven named financiers have probably already picked contractors, and GreenLancer says it already serves seven financiers. | How this version avoids them: GreenLancer, Atma, Revival, ECG and Optimus earn service fees and have no balance sheet, and none of them buys loans. The seven Freedom Forever financiers and Sunrun/GoodLeap keep their in-house step-in, but they are holders, not buyers, and they are not the sellers this targets. Credit unions, servicers and trusts that want out are the supply. NPL funds lack cure capability. OhmSnap is homeowner lead-gen, Solar Insure sells owner warranties, and Enphase runs a post-PTO upsell. Revenue comes from loan value uplift, not vendor contracts, so it does not depend on beating GreenLancer for a financier relationship. GreenLancer-style shops and local contractors become subcontractors.

title: A Price Reporting Agency for Trade Materials
one_liner: Turn pooled supply-house invoices into contract-grade, SKU-level price evidence for the trades, starting with cost-change certificates that win price-adjustment change orders and ending as the index that escalation clauses and price-lock guarantees reference.
customer: First: plumbing, HVAC and electrical subcontractors with $3-30M revenue that carry fixed-price bids, multi-month jobs and maintenance agreements and eat cost changes between bid and buy. End state: the counterparties who write and argue escalation clauses, meaning general contractors, property owners and managers, municipal procurement, insurers, home-warranty programs, lenders, and the manufacturers and distributors who want realized-price data.
problem: Price adjustment requests are argued with anecdotes. A sub says copper fittings and water heaters are up 15-20% since the bid, and the GC or owner asks for proof. Broad public benchmarks (producer price indices and estimating books) are category-level and lag what contractors actually pay by SKU at their contractor multiplier in their region, and supplier price letters flow to contractors with a long lag, as the parent's tariff research noted (50% Section 232 copper duty from August 1, 2025). Subs either absorb the difference on fixed-price work or lose weeks assembling invoices by hand. There is no independent, contract-grade reference that both sides of a contract accept, as far as the parent's research and I could find. Parent idea limit: a per-shop audit keeps price data private and never becomes anything a counterparty trusts.
solution: Step 1 (months 0-6) sells a Cost-Change Certificate. For a sub with a fixed-price contract or bid, we parse its own supplier invoices and quotes into a SKU-normalized evidence pack: cost at the bid date versus cost at purchase, supplier price-letter references, invoice copies, and the escalation amount calculated by the contract's own formula, reviewed by the shop's accountant. It needs no network on day one, only one shop's invoices. Step 2: every certificate is paid partly in data, since the shop opts in to contribute its anonymized line items to the pool and in exchange gets a free alert feed ('your PEX-A fitting cost is 9% above the regional median'). Step 3 (months 6-18): publish weekly transaction-based indices by category and region, with a 30-day lag, minimum-contributor thresholds, no supplier or shop names, to stay clear of price-signaling and confidentiality problems. Owners, GCs and municipalities start writing 'adjusted per [Index] Copper Fittings, Region' into contracts and pay for verified access. Step 4 (months 18-36): price-lock guarantees for quoted jobs, underwritten off the index through an MGA or reinsurer partner, where shops pay a small premium on covered materials and we carry the basis risk we understand better than anyone.
why_now: Tariff-driven cost swings made price adjustment a routine dispute in 2025-26, and owners and GCs are rewriting price-adjustment language. The barrier to a transaction index was always normalizing hundreds of supplier catalog and invoice formats into comparable SKUs, and LLMs just made that cheap. Field-service and accounting systems make invoice ingestion easy. The volatility also means the certificate solves a painful, dated, dollar-denominated problem today, not a theoretical data project.
revenue_model: Certificates at $250-400 each, or 15-20% of the escalation actually approved (better alignment on big claims). Then index subscriptions of $500-2,000 per month for GCs, owners, insurers and municipal buyers who want verified reference access, with data licensing to manufacturers and distributors for realized-price and sell-through data. Later underwriting margin on price-lock guarantees, priced at roughly 1.5-3% of covered materials. Example: a sub with a $400K contract that is 30% materials and 8% higher-cost has a $9,600 claim, and a 20% success fee on half of that approved is about $1,000 per contract.
non_obvious_insight: In commodity markets the durable business is not the data feed but being the named reference in contracts, which is why price reporting agencies for metals and lumber have switching costs no feed provider has. The way in is not a dashboard. It is a document that ends an argument, sold to the party who is losing money now. The certificate requires no network on day one, and the network appears as a byproduct because every certificate adds contributed data. It is also a position platform vendors and supply houses structurally cannot take. ServiceTitan and Kojo depend on supplier integrations such as Ferguson and Hajoca, and publishing cross-customer price data pits those partners against their users, while a supply house cannot publish its own multipliers.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 light-commercial mechanical and plumbing subs with open fixed-price contracts where costs have risen since bid (owner peer groups, PHCC and ACCA chapters). Build the SKU normalizer for the top 200 SKUs (copper tube and fittings, PEX, PVC, water heaters, gas flex) across Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply, Home Depot Pro and local-house formats. Produce 5 certificates within 2 weeks and record how each GC or owner responds, since approval rate and dollars approved are the key learning. Sign 3 shops to the contingency version. Publish a free monthly 'copper fittings' note from the first shops' data (with disclosure) to seed the brand. Have an attorney review the contribution agreement and the aggregation and lag rules before publishing anything pooled. Web search was unavailable to the parent researcher, so verify that no existing indices or claim-documentation vendors serve this niche.
lineage: mutation of I0068 ('Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags), Kojo, BuildOps (Procurement and Payables), Fergus. White space: Nobody I found offers a contingency-fee, done-for-you recovery audit for trade shops. What remains unserved is the customer-side leak: parts on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or pulled from truck stock, that never reached the customer invoice, plus supplier price drift and quoted-price violations tied back to the shop's own pricebook and markup targets. Existing tools (ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps, Ramp) are software the shop must adopt and operate, and they focus on paying suppliers correctly. Three parts are open: (1) shops on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge or Simpro, or ServiceTitan shops not using Procurement/AP, who have no PO-to-job workflow; (2) the done-for-you, no-recovery-no-fee commercial model, which no software vendor offers; (3) a cross-shop SKU price benchmark from pooled supply-house invoices. I found no evidence anyone has assembled that for residential and light-commercial trade shops. ServiceTitan's Manage Statements and Manage Credits are the closest overlap with the returns-credit and price-error pieces. | How this version avoids them: ServiceTitan AP, Kojo's Sourcing Grid, BuildOps, Ramp and MarginEdge all keep price data private per customer to help that customer buy or pay better. None produces a third-party-verifiable, cross-shop reference that a counterparty accepts, and none sells to GCs, owners, insurers or municipalities. Platform vendors will not publish it because it turns their supplier integration partners (Ferguson is a named ServiceTitan integration) into adversaries. Kojo focuses on larger commercial contractors' purchasing, while this works from the invoices of any shop regardless of field-service software, so Housecall Pro, Jobber and FieldEdge shops are included without any adoption. It also moves the monetization away from the crowded supplier-invoice audit toward evidence and a standard, where the incumbents have no product.

title: Aftermarket Support for Stranded DJI Fleets
one_liner: Repair, rebuilt batteries, parts and firmware-independence retrofits for the many legally owned DJI drones that can no longer be replaced with new models.
customer: Police and fire drone units, agricultural spray operators, land surveyors, roofing and solar inspectors, and small public-safety departments with grant money.
problem: The FCC barred new DJI and Autel models in December 2025, US drone tariffs took effect in September 2026 (component tariffs follow in 2027), and China's export controls now cover motors, batteries, radios and sensors. Existing fleets stay legal to fly but face scarce parts and no assured US repair path.
solution: A US repair depot with stocked parts, rebuilt batteries using allied-source cells, gimbal and camera swaps, and open flight-controller retrofits (ArduPilot/PX4) as a migration path. Offer a per-drone maintenance plan with predictive service, and trade-in credits toward US-made airframes, which also become a lead source for those makers.
why_now: The December 2025 FCC action, September 2026 tariffs and export controls all landed within a year. The installed base is large and aging, and no one has a business focused on serving it.
revenue_model: $150-800 per repair, $30-80 per drone per month for maintenance plans, battery and parts sales, and referral fees from US airframe makers on trade-ins.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone debates who replaces DJI, while nobody serves the installed base for the next 5 years. Service earns higher margin than building a competing airframe, starts faster, and gives you the customer list every US-made airframe maker wants.
first_30_days: Buy 20 broken Mavic and Matrice units on secondary markets and set up a bench. Pitch fixed-price maintenance plans to 30 sheriff drone units and agricultural spraying co-ops, and sell the first 10 plans.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: DJI (own repair, DJI Care, Authorized Service Centers via CarePro Technology Inc), Drone Nerds (plus Drone Nerds Enterprise), Dronefly, BRINC (Safeguard Program). White space: The claim that nobody serves the installed base is wrong. DJI/CarePro, Drone Nerds, Dronefly and small independents already repair DJI drones, and Drone Nerds already sells enterprise hot-swap and always-flying plans. The gap is capacity and guaranteed turnaround. Repair waits reportedly went from days to about three months (https://dronexl.co/2026/09/01/fcc-covered-list-panel-uav-expo-repair-times/), and replacement hardware takes 6-9 weeks. What looks unserved: (1) A US depot with a real SLA (about 72 hours) and loaner pools for Matrice, Mavic 3 Enterprise and Agras spray fleets, sold as overflow capacity to backlogged authorized centers and resellers as well as directly. (2) Agricultural spray operators: DJI has roughly 80% of US spray-drone sales and cumulative tariffs have tripled prices (about $20k to $100k), so these fleets have no affordable replacement (https://dronexl.co/2025/12/17/connecticut-ag-drone-law-tariffs-ban/). FCC docket 26-189 also targets economic-poison spraying drones for retroactive action. (3) Rebuilt batteries from allied-source cells: I found no one doing this at scale, but DJI smart-battery lockouts make it technically uncertain, and I could not check that. (4) Parts stockpiling ahead of the component tariffs that start 2027-02-09. (5) Buying retired fleets from agencies that are switching, for refurbish, resale and parts harvest; El Paso's chief said the department will dispose of its DJI equipment once replacements arrive. The open ArduPilot/PX4 retrofit has no precedent or demand signal that I found. It also does not remove the DJI camera, gimbal and radio modules, so it does not fix compliance. It is the weakest part of the idea.

title: Graduate Pay Ledger for CDL Schools and Carriers
one_liner: CDL schools get the verified placement and earnings evidence Workforce Pell requires by having graduates upload settlement stubs to a pay-verification app. Carriers pay to reach those graduates with verified pay pages, and lenders pay for stub-based income packets.
customer: Small and mid-size CDL schools and other short-program providers (paying per completer verified) as the beachhead. Carriers with 50-1,000 trucks that pay $6-15k to hire a driver (verified-pay badge and graduate funnel), mortgage and auto lenders serving drivers, and state workforce boards.
problem: Workforce Pell requires verified placement (about 70%) with a clock that starts before the governor application, and CDL schools typically track completion, not employment. State wage records lag by quarters and miss owner-operators and per-diem pay. Meanwhile the pay-verification app has a cold-start problem: recruiting drivers one Facebook group at a time is slow and noisy.
solution: At completion, schools enroll graduates in the pay app. In exchange for a verified profile and a small incentive, graduates upload their first settlement stubs at 30, 90 and 180 days. The AI extracts employer, paid miles, deadhead, detention and pay per hour away from home. The school gets an audit-ready placement and earnings ledger, the governor application packet, and an earnings-premium exposure score. Carriers that look good buy a Verified Pay page and a graduate applicant funnel, and lenders buy income packets built from stubs.
why_now: Workforce Pell went live for provider approvals in 2026 and the placement and completion evidence rules make this a compliance purchase with a deadline. The stub-parsing AI is cheap now. Carriers are paying up to $15k per driver hired and are locked out of trust because drivers only believe stubs.
revenue_model: $150-300 per completer verified or $4-12k per year per program. $3-5k for a governor application packet. $1.5-3k earnings-premium exposure report. $500-3,000 per month carrier subscriptions for verified pay pages and graduate funnel. $300-1,000 lender referral fees per funded loan. Free for graduates.
non_obvious_insight: A settlement stub proves placement, employer, and earnings in a single document that drivers, carriers and lenders already trust, which employer-email verification and state wage matching can't do for small carriers or per-diem pay. The school-by-carrier pay matrix is a data product in its own right. It tells each school which carriers to steer graduates toward, which raises next year's placement rate and protects Pell eligibility, so verification pays for itself in outcomes.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 CDL schools in two states that have opened Workforce Pell approval, at a $1.5k pilot price. Backfill the last 12 months of completers by text, asking for stubs, to produce a baseline verified placement rate and a sample governor packet. Publish a 'State of Real Pay for New CDL Graduates' report naming carriers. Sell Verified Pay badges to the 3-5 mid-size fleets that hire the most graduates and sign one bank-statement mortgage broker for lender leads.
lineage: hybrid of I0916 + I0227 (Placement Proof for Workforce Pell Providers + Verified Pay Receipts for Truck Driver Hiring). Why stronger: Placement Proof alone has to chase completers by text and email, and the pay app alone has a slow consumer cold start. Combined, schools deliver a captive, motivated cohort of new drivers every month, the pay data comes from the exact graduates schools need to verify, and carriers and lenders subsidize a verification service that schools would otherwise pay for entirely themselves.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ellucian (incl. former Anthology CampusNexus SIS, Occupation Insight), Populi, Gradelink, Lightcast. White space: Confidence is LOW. My WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) before any searches ran. Only 9 direct page fetches went through, and they returned homepage-level content. I also tried a Google URL through WebFetch and then stopped, because that was an attempt to get around the search limit. I found no direct competitor, but I did not search for one, so this is not evidence that none exists. Homepage checks of Populi, Ellucian/Anthology, Gradelink and Lightcast showed no Workforce Pell or placement-verification features. Orbund's site was bot-blocked, and the Federal Register and ed.gov pages redirected or returned 403, so I could not check the rule text. Likely unserved wedge: a Workforce Pell-specific product that (1) backfills the 12-month look-back by contacting completers and employers, (2) reconciles evidence to the rule's placement definition, and (3) produces the governor application packet for small CDL, CNA, barbering and cosmetology schools. Not searched, so still unknown: startups or Product Hunt and YC entries; existing placement-verification services already sold to accredited career schools (ACCSC, NACCAS, COE reporting); consultancies selling this as a service; state-built portals; and SIS vendor Workforce Pell roadmaps. Structural risks visible without further research: (a) if the final rule lets states verify placement from UI wage records, a self-collected pay-stub product loses much of its value; (b) SIS vendors can bolt this on as a feature; (c) the number of approved programs, and so the buyer count, may be small at first. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TruckersReport (carrier reviews and salary survey), Best Fleets to Drive For (CarriersEdge), Tenstreet (Driver Pulse, IntelliApp, Hiring Center), Drive My Way. White space: Web search was unavailable (the session's 200-search budget was used up), so this rests on about 25 direct page fetches plus prior knowledge. Confidence is moderate to low. A reviewer should re-run searches for 'verified driver pay', 'settlement stub scanner' and 'trucker mortgage per diem' before committing.

I found no product that does all of this: (1) collect settlement stubs, (2) verify them with fraud checks, and (3) publish per-carrier, receipts-backed effective pay, including dollars per hour away from home. The closest, TruckersReport, has an unverified self-reported salary survey run by a site paid by carriers' recruiting budgets. Best Fleets to Drive For is survey-based. Tenstreet and Drive My Way own recruiting flow but show no pay-verification product.

Specific unserved gaps:
- A trust-backed pay number that uses stubs as proof, computed as dollars per hour on the road rather than per mile.
- Lease-purchase and owner-operator drivers, whose settlements are itemized and who are the most exposed to deceptive ads.
- A stub-based income packet that handles per-diem structures for non-QM and bank-statement lenders. Truv and Argyle verify through payroll connections and are not built for per-diem trucker income.

Weak points that could still sink it:
1. Cold start and selection bias. Unhappy drivers upload more, and carriers with a bad median will not buy a badge. A pay-for-badge model also has a credibility conflict.
2. Stubs do not show time away from home. Hours-away metrics need driver-entered dates or ELD integration, which is hard.
3. The truth-in-leasing itemized-settlement rule (49 CFR 376.12) applies to owner-operator leases, not W-2 company drivers. The idea's 'raw material already exists' claim is only partly true. I could not fetch the regulation this session.
4. Publishing rankings of named carriers invites legal threats. Self-published analytics are not covered by Section 230 the way user reviews are.
5. Per-funded-loan referral fees to a non-lender may run into RESPA Section 8, so this needs counsel. Lenders will also likely re-verify borrower-supplied stubs, which limits the lender product's value. This is from prior knowledge and not verified.

title: Herd Roll-Forward: Lender-Paid Cattle Collateral Reconciliation
one_liner: Sell ag lenders a loan covenant that rebuilds the borrower's herd from paper that third parties generated (vet records, sale-barn settlements, brand certificates, tag and vaccine purchases) and flags loans where expected head and claimed head do not reconcile.
customer: Wedge: the chief credit officer and senior ag lender at one Farm Credit association or one $500M-$3B community bank in a brand-inspection state (Nebraska, South Dakota, Montana, Wyoming or the Texas Panhandle). It should carry $50M+ in cow-calf, bred-heifer and heifer-development loans of $500K-$5M. The bank pays, and the cost passes through to the borrower as a collateral inspection fee that lenders already charge. The vet is a paid data source, not the customer.
problem: The parent's own flaws are the problem to fix. A borrower-initiated count means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. A chute-side count proves only what was at the chute that day, not cattle on other leases, cattle sold since, or cattle double-pledged. It says nothing about ownership or lien priority. Vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit. And $2-3/head split with the vet is thin. Meanwhile lenders still rely on drive-by counts and borrower spreadsheets on loans where a 500-cow herd is $1.5M+ of collateral nobody independent has counted.
solution: An annual 'Herd Roll-Forward' per loan that closes an inventory equation: last year's verified head + expected calf crop (from preg-check records) + purchases (sale-barn buyer settlements, health certificates) - sales (consignor settlements, brand and feedyard closeouts) - deaths = expected ending head. That figure is compared with the borrower's claimed head and any chute-side scan. A second check triangulates consumables: EID tags bought, vaccine doses and dewormer from the vet, mineral and hay purchases, and grazing-lease animal-unit-months, all versus claimed head. The borrower signs one information-rights rider at loan closing, which lets the vet, sale barns, brand agency and feed suppliers release records to us. That rider is what removes adverse selection: the loan agreement opts the borrower in, not the borrower. LLM extraction reads the messy PDFs and photos. The vet is one attestor, contracted narrowly ('I handled N head with these IDs on this date', no collateral opinion) and paid a flat $150-300 per session for exporting the sheet they already made and one-tap signing. The lender gets a variance flag, a lien and ownership panel (UCC or state central-filing search plus brand records) and a portfolio dashboard.
why_now: (1) Reading hundreds of differently formatted settlement statements, invoices and health papers used to take an analyst hours per loan, and LLM document extraction has cut that to cents. That is the cost-stack collapse that makes reconciliation cheaper than a drive-by. (2) Federal EID tag rules for many interstate cattle movements (Nov 2024) mean more animals carry digital IDs and more vets and barns hold exportable records. (3) Record cattle prices are pushing herd rebuilding onto debt, with bred cows around $3,000+, so each loan carries big collateral. Lenders are also carrying delinquencies, and a fresh cattle-collateral fraud case (claimed in the parent, unverified) is prompting loan-committee questions. (4) It is fall, when preg-checks, weaning and calf sales generate the documents, and December-February annual renewals are when banks decide on inspections.
revenue_model: The bank pays per loan per year: about $600 under $1M, $1,500 for $1-3M and $3,000 above $3M, roughly 5-10 bps of balance. A portfolio dashboard is $1,000-2,000/month at 100+ loans. A bank with 120 cattle loans is worth about $130K-180K/yr. Vets get a flat per-session data fee, so their cost does not scale with head count. Target gross margin is 70%+ once extraction is automated, with human review only on flagged loans. Later add anonymized county and herd-size variance benchmarks for credit committees and examiners.
non_obvious_insight: Do not count the cattle, count the paper. Every animal movement leaves a record in a third party's hands (barn, brand inspector, vet, feed store, feedyard), and fraud shows up as arithmetic that does not close. Counting heads is the least informative check, so the chute day is a calibration anchor rather than the product. This also makes the vet's reluctance irrelevant, since any attestor or document set works, and it turns the borrower's own suppliers into the fraud detectors.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-2: run 12 interviews (5 loan officers or credit officers, 3 vets, 2 barn clerks, 2 brand inspectors). Ask each bank who does its inspections now and what it costs, and search for existing third-party collateral inspectors. Weeks 2-3: get one bank to pick 15 existing borrowers up for renewal and get consent. Manually reconcile each from documents the borrower already holds (sale settlements, preg-check sheets, vet invoices, tag orders) and from one vet's exports. Charge $500 per loan, or waive the fee for the first five if the bank agrees to write down what it learned. Week 4: present the variance results to the bank's ag loan committee, especially any loan that did not close. Convert the result into a one-page 'inventory information rights' rider for new bred-heifer and operating-line loans, priced at $750-1,500 per loan.
lineage: mutation of I0338 ('Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global / Where Food Comes From (Beef Passport), Merck Animal Health (Allflex tags/readers, Vence). White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. I did direct fetches of about 15 vendor and agency pages, plus GitHub repo searches. Nothing here rules out a direct competitor. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.

What the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. Every one of them is a producer-side management or supply-chain tool. GitHub searches turned up no open-source lender-verification tool, only hobby herd apps.

The unserved wedge is a lender-mandated, third-party-attested herd inventory built as a covenant workflow. It would cover the vet-signed chute-side count, a portfolio dashboard, and year-over-year anomaly flags such as head count down, pregnancy rate down, or tags missing versus last year.

Structural weaknesses to be skeptical of:
- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.
- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.
- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.
- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.
- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature. | How this version avoids them: CattleMax, AgriWebb, Gallagher, Merck/Allflex and Vence, HerdDogg, Halter and Ceres Tag are all producer-paid management or hardware tools. A borrower-paid tool sees only what the borrower records, and those vendors cannot audit the customers who pay them. IMI Global's Beef Passport verifies supply-chain claims for a producer-paid program, not cross-counterparty reconciliation or a covenant workflow. We are lender-paid and source-agnostic, and we ingest their CSV exports as just one input, so they become feeders rather than rivals. Their incumbent asymmetry is real: adding lender variance reports means telling their own paying customers they are now audited. The remaining risk is unknown third-party inspection firms, which the interviews must surface, and a possible white-label deal with IMI or an EID vendor.

title: The Pharmacy-Verified Reimbursement Index
one_liner: A furnisher-funded bureau, like a credit bureau for PBM payments, that turns what pharmacies actually pay and are actually paid into a reference index that state laws, Medicaid rate-setting and transparent-PBM contracts can cite, launching with a per-state Underwater Index sold to pharmacy associations for the 2027 legislative sessions.
customer: First six months: state pharmacy associations and their legal and lobbying arms in 3-5 states with active 2027 PBM agendas, at $25-60k per state per year. Next: state Medicaid pharmacy programs and state employee plans rebasing dispensing fees and ingredient-cost basis, departments of insurance enforcing below-cost and pay-parity laws, and TPAs, consultants and transparent PBMs that want an external yardstick. Eventually: contracts that reference the index directly. Contributing pharmacies pay nothing and get a dividend.
problem: Everyone who needs a reference price for pharmacy reimbursement relies on an interested party or a slow survey. NADAC is a voluntary survey of acquisition costs that says nothing about dispensing cost or what any PBM actually paid. State cost-of-dispensing studies are periodic, commissioned from consultants, and stale by publication (typically low-to-mid six figures each; verify). Legislators cannot say how many claims are paid below cost or by whom, so reimbursement-floor and pay-parity laws are enforced only by complaint. PBMs face no neutral definition of a fair payment. The parent's insight (pharmacies hold the ground-truth ledger) is stronger as infrastructure than as a one-off audit.
solution: Pharmacies use the free local-first margin report (same ingestion as a per-pharmacy tool) and opt in to contribute monthly aggregates: paid price and invoice cost per NDC per PBM network per state, plus optionally allocated cost-to-dispense. The bureau publishes: (a) a State Underwater Index (share of claims paid below acquisition cost, by PBM, only where 10+ pharmacies and 5+ per PBM cell contribute, with a 90-day lag); (b) an invoice-based acquisition cost index by NDC-week; (c) a quarterly cost-of-dispensing panel; (d) a regulator API to test whether a network paid below the index in a given month. Design floor for antitrust: a third-party-run exchange following the withdrawn 1996 health-care information-exchange conditions (5+ contributors, no contributor over 25% weight, data 3+ months old), plus counsel sign-off. Credibility: published methodology, an independent standards board (pharmacist, health economist, antitrust counsel, ex-regulator) and a sample audit by an accounting firm. Flywheel: an association buys the evidence pack, a law cites the index, the regulator needs the feed, contracts reference the index, and more pharmacies contribute for the dividend (25% of index revenue, pro rata by verified contribution).
why_now: A wave of state PBM reimbursement and transparency laws has arrived just as closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens closing about 1,200 stores, Drug Channels' August 2026 'K-shaped shakeout') give legislators a reason to demand numbers; 2027 sessions open in January and associations need evidence in Q4. The cost stack has collapsed: surveying a few hundred pharmacies by questionnaire costs six figures, but reading remits and invoices they already hold costs cents per claim now that OCR and LLM parsing handle messy formats and local-first processing removes the custody objection. This is a 2026 unlock, not a 2019 one.
revenue_model: Association evidence pack plus monthly index: $25-60k per state per year (target 3 states by month 6, about $100-150k). State Medicaid and employee-plan data licenses: $100-400k per state per year after a track record. DOI compliance feed: $50-150k. API licenses for TPAs, consultants and transparent PBMs: $25-100k. Index-in-contract licensing: about $0.02-0.05 per member per month, comparable to index-licensing models in other markets. Pharmacies: free plus a 25% revenue dividend. A 30-state footprint could plausibly support $10-30M a year.
non_obvious_insight: Standards win by being cited in statutes and contracts, and NADAC became the reference by being neutral, not by being complete. A pharmacy-verified index earns legitimacy differently, because it comes from invoices and remits (facts, not survey opinion), and it is the only source that can measure paid versus cost per PBM, which is exactly what a below-cost reimbursement law needs in order to be enforced. Associations fund the first index as lobbying evidence, the resulting laws then create a compliance buyer (the regulator), and each citation adds switching cost. The more PBM-owned pharmacies dominate the market, the more the independents' ledger is the only independent counterfactual.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick 2 states with an active 2027 PBM agenda and pitch the association executive directors: 'your state's Underwater Report by December 15 for session prep, co-branded.' Days 5-25: recruit 25 contributing pharmacies per state with a free margin report; run 6 months of remits and invoices through a local script by hand (concierge). Days 10-20: retain antitrust counsel for a 10-page methodology and thresholds memo, and seat a 5-person advisory board. Day 20-30: ask a state DOI or Medicaid pharmacy director for a 30-minute meeting on what they would need to enforce existing rules. By day 30: 2 signed letters of intent at about $25k and 40 contributing pharmacies. By day 60: first anonymized state index published. Kill criterion: no association will pay $25k for a state report before the session opens.
lineage: mutation of I1266 ('Pharmacy-Side PBM Ledger for Employers'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Truveris (truAudit / truGuard / Marketplace), Capital Rx (Judi Health), AffirmedRx, SmithRx. White space: Caveat on confidence: my WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I ran any query in this session. The verdict rests on direct fetches of about 20 competitor and source pages plus GitHub searches, not on a broad landscape scan. It is a provisional 'gap', not a confirmed one.

What I did not find: no company that ingests pharmacy-side remits, benchmarks per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement against a peer pool, models Q4 network offers, and ties pharmacy-paid amounts to an employer's PBM claims file. The employer-side audit market is served: Truveris, benefits consultants, and transparent PBMs that market pass-through. Their audits appear to start from what the PBM hands over, and I found no sign they hold the pharmacy-paid half.

The pharmacy-side gap is plausible. PioneerRx, PQS and CPESN pages show no reimbursement-benchmarking or contract-modeling feature. Not verified: pharmacy services administrative organizations (PSAOs such as Cardinal, AmerisourceBergen Elevate, AAP, Health Mart Atlas) and pharmacy management system vendors may already offer contract review or reimbursement reports to members. Confirm this in customer interviews before building, because the PSAOs negotiate PBM contracts and already hold members' remits.

The specific unserved wedge is a claim-level reconciliation between the pharmacy's actual paid amount and the employer's PBM claims file, delivered as a spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member.

Risks that shrink the white space:
- PBM provider-manual confidentiality clauses and possible antitrust or information-exchange concerns when pooling competitors' reimbursement rates.
- Getting employer PBM claims files with sponsor consent.
- Pharmacy remits are not uniformly 835 files.
- The January 2027 contract window is roughly 3 months away and cannot be met by a product built from scratch. | How this version avoids them: Truveris and other employer-audit firms analyze PBM-supplied claims for individual clients; this sells neutral reference data to governments, associations and payers, and those firms can be licensees. Capital Rx, AffirmedRx and SmithRx market transparency but cannot certify it themselves, so the index is a potential licensed yardstick for them. rx-gap-finder is a one-pharmacy tool with no pool, no network effect and no legitimacy with regulators. PQS/EQUIPP holds 65,000 connected pharmacies but sells adherence and quality to plans, and adding payer-adverse reimbursement data would strain those relationships (hypothesis, unverified). CPESN's 3,500 pharmacies are a contribution channel. 46brooklyn's public research is a natural academic advisor or co-publisher, not a substitute, because it cannot see paid amounts. Gap in the parent's competitor scan: state cost-of-dispensing survey vendors and the CMS NADAC contractor were not researched, so verify whether they are building continuous invoice-based products before committing.

title: Independent Collateral Verifier for Warehouse Lenders
one_liner: Sell the same listing-vs-ledger signal not to the floorplan lender but to the lender's lender: credit funds and banks that fund floorplan and subprime auto lenders and get a borrower-supplied VIN tape they have never been able to check, delivered as a signed monthly verification certificate that borrowers pay for through facility fees.
customer: Portfolio-monitoring and credit officers at credit funds, banks and specialty-finance desks that provide warehouse or revolving lines to independent floorplan companies and subprime or BHPH auto lenders. The chooser is the warehouse lender, and the payer is usually the borrower via a monitoring fee written into the facility, the way custodian and backup-servicer fees already are. The law firms that draft these credit agreements are a second influence channel.
problem: After Tricolor and PrimaLend (Sept 2025), the lender's lender is exposed to collateral that is self-reported by the party with the strongest incentive to overstate it. It receives a VIN-level borrowing-base tape weekly or monthly. It has no auditors and no view into dealers, and field exams are annual, sample-based and weeks stale. It holds the tape but has no line of outside data to check it against. Existing floorplan-side tools are bought by the borrower, so they cannot be independent by construction.
solution: Tape-in, verification-out. The warehouse lender (or borrower on its behalf) forwards the borrowing-base tape it already receives and we return a weekly exceptions report and a signed monthly Borrowing Base Verification Certificate. (1) VIN-level reconcile of every tape VIN against listing history and the borrower's reported paydowns and collections, flagging vanished-from-listing with no paydown. (2) A borrower-level Collateral Integrity Index covering percent of tape VINs vanished-unpaid by age bucket, listing coverage ratio, and trend, benchmarked against the warehouse lender's other borrowers. (3) Because noise averages out at portfolio level, precision required is far lower than for per-VIN dispatch, and low listing coverage is reported as its own finding, not hidden. (4) Escalation: a 'for-cause exam recommended' trigger with a shortlist of dealers for a partner field-exam firm. (5) Contract language kit: a standard 'independent verification agent' covenant and fee schedule for law firms to drop into new facilities and amendments.
why_now: Sept 2025's Tricolor and PrimaLend collapses put verification failure in front of every warehouse lender and investor. Private credit funds now hold large slices of specialty-auto warehouse exposure with small monitoring teams. Facilities are being re-papered and re-underwritten, so a verification covenant can go in now instead of waiting for a renewal cycle. Cheap licensed listing history and LLM tape parsing make a weekly external check a software job instead of an exam-firm engagement.
revenue_model: Monitoring fee of about $3,000 to $6,000 per facility per month ($36k to $72k per year), paid by the borrower through the facility's fee schedule or by the lender directly, plus a $15k to $25k onboarding backtest. Add-ons include a 10 to 15 percent referral fee from partner field-exam firms on for-cause exams, and licensing the anonymized Collateral Integrity Index to ABS investors and surveillance teams. If a niche of 100 to 150 specialty-auto warehouse lenders with 3 to 5 facilities each adopts it, the ceiling is roughly 300 to 600 facilities, or $15M to $30M per year before expanding to retail-auto tapes. These figures are assumptions to test.
non_obvious_insight: The funding-side buyer already owns the one input the product needs (the VIN tape) and has never had a single external data point to check it against. Verification fees are set by the chooser but paid by the borrower, who benefits from an independent stamp that supports better advance rates, so the payer wants it even when the chooser only tolerates it. Once written into facility documents, a fee line like custodian and backup servicer is sticky and renews automatically, which is a switching-cost moat that a per-dealer SaaS tool never gets.
first_30_days: Days 1 to 10, list 40 warehouse lenders and credit funds active in specialty auto from trade press and deal announcements, and line up conversations with two or three finance law partners who draft these facilities. Days 10 to 30, run 10 calls with portfolio monitoring heads and offer a free one-facility 'shadow verification' using a tape they already hold. They email it, and within five business days we return a one-page findings memo covering coverage ratio, vanished-unpaid VIN count and peer benchmark. Also sign a partner field-exam firm for for-cause follow-ups. Success is one lender agreeing to a paid quarter and one law firm agreeing to circulate the covenant language.
lineage: mutation of I0218 ('Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: In-house 'website VIN vs floorplan VIN' comparison (SAS Global Forum paper, 'PROC HTTP: Using the Web to Combat Fraud in Auto Finance During a Global Pandemic'), Vero Technologies (VeroOS), SBS Digital Audit (SBS Software), LotCount. White space: Among the products I could find, none sells the specific signal in this idea: an external-behavior signal (a floored VIN vanishing from the dealer site or marketplaces) checked against the lender's own payoff ledger on a running clock, with a ranked daily queue. Existing offerings cover other things. Physical or photo audits (CSI, LotCount, SBS Digital Audit, Netresult) are periodic and dealer-cooperative. Platforms (Vero, Solifi, Alfa, SBS servicing) analyze the lender's own payment and title data. Bank-data tools (Plaid-style) watch dealer cash. DRN covers location. The unserved wedge is mid-size and small lenders that lack data-science teams: independent floorplan companies, credit unions and community banks with dealer lines, and third-party audit firms that need risk-based audit targeting. It is strongest for used-car and buy-here-pay-here dealers, where captives' retail-delivery reports do not exist. Caveats that shrink the white space: (1) captives see retail deliveries within days and can build the signal in-house, and the SAS paper suggests at least one lender did; (2) Vero, SBS and Cox/NextGear could bolt on the signal; (3) a listing that disappears is a noisy signal (wholesaled, transferred, in recon, or the dealer never lists), so precision must be proven; (4) marketplace scraping has terms-of-service risk, so a licensed feed such as MarketCheck is likely needed. | How this version avoids them: Nothing in the competitor set sells to the funding side. Vero, Solifi, Alfa, SBS servicing and NextGear's self-audit are borrower-side tools, so a check the borrower buys from its own vendor is not independent. Cox owns NextGear, Autotrader and Dealertrack, so it is conflicted as a verifier of NextGear's rivals. CSI, LotCount, SBS Digital Audit and Netresult are dealer-level physical audits ordered by the originator, and none delivers a tape-level attestation or a peer-benchmarked index. DRN is a location signal and MOBI is a captive-only pilot. The SAS-paper method could be built by a lender, but the lender's lender lacks the daily floored data and the analytics staff, and buys instead of builds. MarketCheck is the supplier. The portfolio-level unit of analysis also neutralizes the biggest weakness of the parent (per-VIN noise).

title: Phantom-Load Registry: Land Records Meet Utility Queues
one_liner: A utility-funded vetting desk that joins courthouse land-assembly signals with co-op and municipal large-load inquiry logs, so it can say which 100-1,000 MW projects are real and which LLC families are shopping the same megawatts to five utilities.
customer: Electric co-ops, G&Ts, municipal utilities and PUDs with 5-person engineering staffs. They pay per memo or on retainer. Secondary buyers are developers' land teams and site-selection consultants, infrastructure and energy funds buying alt-data, and county economic-development offices.
problem: Every party sees half the picture. A small utility sees the inquiry (an LLC, a MW ask, a PowerPoint) but not the land trail. The land-assembly watcher sees option memoranda and easements but cannot tell a real hyperscale campus from a speculator flipping dirt. Nobody sees the same MW shopped across states. Texas SB 6's collateral rule (final expected by end of 2026) will push phantom load onto softer neighbors.
solution: First product is the fixed-price vetting memo ($7.5-25k) with a red/amber/green result and a recommended security amount. The site-control and LLC-principal items in the 12-point physical-reality test are powered by an image-level read of recorded options, leases and easements, clustered by return-to law firm, notary, signatory and mailing address. Air-permit and equipment-slot checks come from the vetting desk. Utilities that share their inquiry logs (LLC, MW, node, date, outcome) get discounted memos. Those logs become a multi-utility duplicate-request registry that flags land-assembled-but-no-equipment-slot projects and the same LLC family filing at several utilities. Later products are a county-level real-versus-phantom alert feed and alt-data licenses for funds.
why_now: Texas SB 6 (PUCT rule final due by 12/31/2026, $50,000/MW security) is exporting speculators to neighboring states. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or cancelled, so utilities are burned and skeptical. FinCEN's 2025 exemption for domestic companies means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. LLM vision now reads messy scanned instruments accurately.
revenue_model: $7.5-25k per vetting memo. $60-150k per year G&T retainers. $2-8k per month regional developer seats. $750-2,000 per tract title packet. $50-150k per year alt-data licenses for funds. Utilities often pass memo cost to applicants as a study-deposit line item. Later, registry subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Land records show intent, and an option memo is cheap to buy. The equipment and permit trail shows capability. The utility queue shows the ask. No single dataset separates real from speculative, but the join does. Land assembled with no transformer slot, by an LLC family filing at five utilities, is a land flip. Each utility's eventual outcome (built, cancelled, withdrawn) is also a free labeled training set for the tape's classifier, which no scraper competitor can get. Utilities will only share inquiry logs with someone they already trust to vet, and that is a trust position a pure data vendor lacks.
first_30_days: Through state electric cooperative associations, get 3 co-ops to hand over their last 10 inquiries each. Pull 24 months of recorded instruments in those territories, plus state air-permit and LLC filings. Run a free back-test showing which past inquiries were real. Publish a '12 signs your data center inquiry is real' one-pager and send a sample 'who is assembling where' memo to 10 site-selection consultants. Convert 2-3 co-ops to paid $7.5k memos on live inquiries and pitch one G&T retainer.
lineage: hybrid of I0773 + I0079 (Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure + Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities). Why stronger: The vetting desk alone is a services business with a thin data moat, and the tape alone fights for alt-data budgets with no ground-truth labels. Together, memo revenue funds data collection, utility outcomes label the data, and the pooled duplicate registry gets more valuable with each utility that joins. ACV rises, and utilities can be reached through co-op associations instead of cold outreach.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ATTOM Data, Reonomy, Regrid, Enverus. White space: The specific product in the idea, a feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements from county recorders, classifies them from the image rather than the clerk's label, clusters LLC families by notary, return-to firm and address, and alerts on assembly patterns, was not found at any vendor I could read. Everything I could read is adjacent. Parcel and ownership vendors (Regrid, ATTOM, Reonomy) sell deeds, mortgages and LLC piercing but not options or easements. Siting and diligence vendors (Paces, Enverus, GridCARE) help a client find its own site. Project trackers (Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, Data Center Watch) start at permit or public news. Land-management vendors (Pandell, Enverus LandScape) manage a client's own documents. What remains open is cross-county, image-level reading of recorded non-deed instruments to detect other parties' assembly, sold as alerts. It is plausibly protected by the hard part, which is getting recorder access county by county, not the ML. The main structural doubts I could not test are whether developers actually record option memoranda before announcement, and how many counties allow bulk commercial pulls of document images. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GridUnity, Clean Power Research (PowerClerk), Enverus, LandGate. White space: I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check.

title: Materials-Leakage Diligence for Trade-Shop Acquirers
one_liner: Sell search-fund, independent-sponsor and roll-up buyers of plumbing/HVAC shops a five-day report that reconciles the target's supplier spend to its customer invoices, sizes the fixable leak as EBITDA, and sets the baseline for a post-close capture program.
customer: Search-fund CEOs, independent sponsors and PE platform add-on teams buying residential plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops with $2-15M revenue, plus the SBA and ETA lenders and small quality-of-earnings shops that can white-label it. They are repeat or well-networked buyers who already spend on diligence and want a differentiated, quantified edge.
problem: Lower-middle-market trade deals are underwritten from a QuickBooks P&L and a seller-prepared add-back schedule. Gross margin looks acceptable or off, but the buyer cannot tell whether materials margin is real, leaking through unbilled truck-stock parts, or dragged by supplier price drift and stale pricebooks. Buyers discover the leak after closing, when the owner-operator's habits are theirs to fix. The parent idea has the same structural flaws sold to shop owners: owners feel a $10K fee is expensive and resist behavior change, and recoveries are hard to attribute. Generic accounting-firm quality-of-earnings work is done at general-ledger level, as far as I can tell, and rarely reconciles supplier spend to customer invoice lines, especially for shops this small.
solution: A fixed-scope, five-business-day 'Materials Truth Report' run in confirmatory diligence. The seller shares read-only QuickBooks and a field-service invoice export through the data room. The report gives (1) 24 months of Materials Capture Ratio (materials billed at cost divided by materials purchased) by job type, tech and supplier, compared with a pooled peer range; (2) supplier price position, meaning multiplier drift, surcharges and unclaimed credits versus the shop's own history; (3) truck-stock and inventory reasonableness; (4) a normalized gross-margin range for EBITDA underwriting; and (5) a 100-day capture plan with dollar values by lever (kit-based pricebook fixes, tech coaching, repricing file, supplier renegotiation). After closing, the buyer keeps the shop on a capture program measured against the diligence baseline, which was agreed pre-close and so cannot be disputed. Roll-ups get a portfolio dashboard comparing all acquired shops.
why_now: Tariff-driven cost swings since 2025 made materials margin the least trustworthy line in a trade shop's books, and buyers have been burned. HVAC and plumbing are consistently among the most-targeted sectors for search funds, independent sponsors and PE add-ons, so diligence differentiation is now a buyer priority. LLM parsing of supplier lines lets a two-person team deliver in a week what would otherwise be weeks of associate time. Field-service and accounting platforms expose exports, so a seller can share data in minutes.
revenue_model: Buyer pays $7,500 per target ($2,500 at engagement, $5,000 at close, or the full fee if delivered with the deal dead, negotiable). Post-close, either 20% of measured uplift over the diligence baseline for 12 months, or $500 per shop per month for roll-up portfolio monitoring. White-label to QoE boutiques and lenders at $3,000 wholesale per report. Value logic for the buyer: on a $6M shop, one point of revenue is $60K of EBITDA, worth roughly $200-350K of purchase price at 3.5-6x, so a $7.5K report is a rounding error next to the price adjustment or the 100-day plan value it produces.
non_obvious_insight: Changing the payer fixes three flaws at once. Authority: a new owner can change technician compensation, pricebook and process on day one, while an incumbent owner-operator rarely will. Attribution: the diligence baseline is a pre-agreed, third-party measurement, so uplift fees are not disputable. Willingness to pay: to a buyer the leak is enterprise value, not annual cash, so it justifies fees that would scare a shop owner. It also reverses the sales problem. Instead of selling to thousands of busy owners, you sell repeatedly to a few hundred networked buyers who talk to each other in search-fund and independent-sponsor communities, and each diligence adds a shop to the pooled benchmark without a per-shop sales effort. Roll-ups are the natural repeat customer and the natural distribution channel for the capture program.
first_30_days: Build a list of 40 search-fund and independent-sponsor buyers with live trade-shop deals (newsletters, ETA communities, LinkedIn, broker teasers). Offer the report free on one live deal in return for permission to cite anonymized findings. Aim for 3 live deals by day 30, with delivery within 5 business days of data access. In parallel, talk to two small QoE shops about white-labeling. Convert the first paid engagement on the next deal at $7,500. Position it as confirmatory diligence after an LOI, since sellers resist sharing invoice lines pre-LOI. Track whether the median target shows a capture gap worth more than $100K of EBITDA-equivalent, which tells you if buyers will keep paying. Web search was unavailable to the parent researcher, so first check for any existing tech-enabled trade diligence vendors.
lineage: mutation of I0068 ('Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags), Kojo, BuildOps (Procurement and Payables), Fergus. White space: Nobody I found offers a contingency-fee, done-for-you recovery audit for trade shops. What remains unserved is the customer-side leak: parts on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or pulled from truck stock, that never reached the customer invoice, plus supplier price drift and quoted-price violations tied back to the shop's own pricebook and markup targets. Existing tools (ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps, Ramp) are software the shop must adopt and operate, and they focus on paying suppliers correctly. Three parts are open: (1) shops on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge or Simpro, or ServiceTitan shops not using Procurement/AP, who have no PO-to-job workflow; (2) the done-for-you, no-recovery-no-fee commercial model, which no software vendor offers; (3) a cross-shop SKU price benchmark from pooled supply-house invoices. I found no evidence anyone has assembled that for residential and light-commercial trade shops. ServiceTitan's Manage Statements and Manage Credits are the closest overlap with the returns-credit and price-error pieces. | How this version avoids them: ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps and Ramp all sell operating software to the shop, which must adopt it, keep POs and receipts clean, and run it weekly. This is a one-time attested analysis sold to the buyer, produced from an export of whatever field-service system and QuickBooks the target already uses, so nothing has to be adopted and it works on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge and ServiceTitan targets alike. ServiceTitan's statement and credit tools overlap only on the supplier-side piece, which here is a secondary section, not the product. No platform vendor has any incentive to produce third-party diligence on a shop being sold to a competitor, and MarginEdge-style tools are restaurant-only. The buyer relationship also gives a natural route into the parent's capture program after close without selling to the shop from scratch.
